subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, May 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lang that Bill C-17, respecting the reorganization of Air Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I began speaking on Bill C-17 on Friday, May 27, and I consider the present opportunity to continue my remarks a privilege. I am pleased to speak this morning, but was not pleased to note the contents of Bill C-17 dealing with the reorganization of Air Canada. The bill would give the cabinet almost total control of Air Canada, and this raises some serious questions. Since many of us doubt this government's capacity to govern, we must ask, what will be the future of Air Canada? One could not ask this question at a more appropriate time, since this year Air Canada celebrates the fortieth year of its founding. Now the government, as precipitate as an unguided missile, wants to remove Air Canada from the control of CNR. It is on a false course. The government says it will rid Air Canada of its debt load; in other words, it is responding to what Air Canada officials have not been saying, that the airline could make a profit if relieved of the burden of debt. But that is the song of many Crown corporations: they say, "We could make a profit if only we could be free of the rules governing private industry". They want the taxpayer to assume their debts, or their interest charges. They say that if only they were relieved of those burdens, they could make a profit. I shall put before the House figures to show that Air Canada is operating at a loss, and at the same time operating under rules and conditions not available to any other private air carrier on this continent.
Bill C-17 is designed to relieve Air Canada of its debt carrying charges and to give the governor in council direct control of the airline. It is the opinion of Air Canada officials that the airline could show a profit if it were relieved of interest charges on debt. This is just another example of a Crown corporation telling Canadians it could compete with private industry if only it were not forced to abide by the rules governing the private sector. In truth, Air Canada has a heavy
debt load for one good reason, gross mismanagement. The former minister of transport, Hon. Jean Marchand, surely must have had Air Canada in mind when he said the Department of Transport was in a mess.
Air Canada has been awarded the most lucrative routes in this country. I am thinking, for example, of the Toronto-Ottawa-Montreal triangle. Many members of parliament fly one of these routes almost weekly and they cannot help observing, I suggest, that flights in the Toronto-Ottawa-Montreal triangle are virtually filled. Yet on those very flights Air Canada managed to lose almost $19 million last year, for some unknown reason. The aircraft were full, but the airline managed to lose money. I say without hesitation that Air Canada robs one of our major private airlines, CP Air, of the opportunity for lucrative runs in this country. Air Canada lost $19 million on the Toronto-Ottawa-Montreal triangle. CP Air also lost money in the last two years. But we should note two things. The amount of loss was not nearly as significant as Air Canada's. Also, CP Air has been awarded less lucrative routes in Canada, whereas Air Canada has been awarded more lucrative runs from which it should show a profit, not a loss. It lost more money than CP Air.
Compare Air Canada's performance, Mr. Speaker, with that of any major United States airline. What will you find? You will note that virtually every major United States airline made a profit last year. By contrast, Canada's national airline last year ran up some $20 million of debt; and that debt does not include losses incurred with respect to the operation of our airports. If you add our airport debt to that incurred by Air Canada, lump the two together and call them Canada's national air debt, you will arrive at an astronomical figure. Mirabel alone lost $56 million last year. This country lost $110 million on that abortion at Pickering, on that project which put public money through a paper-shredder. The authorities attempted to build an airport where one should never have been built. Our airports have lost millions of dollars. That raises this question: If the government has not the capacity to run airports, has it the capacity to run an airline?
Bill C-17 would vest control of Air Canada in the government. The intention is to sever the airline from its parent Crown corporation, CNR, and place it under the direct control of the Ministry of Transport. Mr. Speaker, a decade ago this country's Post Office showed a profit. Last year the Post Office spilled public money, running up a deficit of $700 million. If one compares the record of Crown corporations, of government administered businesses, with that of corporations in the private sector, one thing becomes clear: their performance is in no way comparable. In almost all instances Crown

May 31, 1977
Air Canada
corporations have run up losses. They have been an albatross around the neck of the taxpayers.
If a private company loses money for an extended time, it goes out of business or is taken over by a competitor. The Post Office managed to turn its previous profit into a loss last year of $700 million. The question is: Do we want the mentality which runs the Post Office to run the operation of this nation's airline? Is that how we want our airline administered? At present, the prospect of an ugly Post Office strike looms like a shadow over the public. There is also the prospect of a Post Office deficit larger than last year's $700 million. In years to come the Post Office could lose much more money. We have in this country some 1,200 state-owned businesses which cost this country's taxpayers $21 billion. Since our population is around 23 million, it is fairly simple to calculate how much it costs the average Canadian to run these state-owned businesses in Canada.
While Air Canada is a malignant debt on the public, the United States airlines south of the border operate at a profit and with better service. It is also interesting to note that in the United States luggage usually arrives on the same plane as the person. Northwestern Airlines, a privately-owned United States company with a similar amount of capital, a similar number of planes and a similar number of miles flown on routes as Air Canada, earned a profit last year of $100 million. By comparison, Air Canada in that same period showed a net loss of $20 million. As I said before, it is simply an albatross around the neck of the Canadian people.
The big difference between Air Canada and Northwest Airlines in the United States is that Air Canada has almost double the staff. That reflects the crux of the whole issue. When you think of the psychological mentality of the civil servants, or the staff in the Crown corporations, you see that their reward is quite different from that of the private sector. When you work in the public service you are rewarded for dreaming up a new idea. If that idea means that somehow more money can be spent, you are rewarded. That is how you get to go from a clerk 1 to a clerk 2 to clerk 3 to clerk 5. That is the way you go up in the branch from supervisor to director to associate deputy minister and on through the chain of command.
In the private sector, there is a very different kind of reward. In the private sector you must demonstrate some form of efficiency in order to work your way up. So it is that on one hand we have an airline virtually the same size, with the same capital investment, the same number of miles flown, and the same number of planes as Air Canada, with a $100 million profit while the state-owned Air Canada has a $20 million deficit hanging around its neck.
This makes us wonder about the whole question of government getting more and more deeply into the private sector, which Bill C-17 intends to do with Air Canada by putting it under direct control of the cabinet. One truly has to ponder the wisdom of that when you look at the $8 billion committed to

the PetroCan nightmare. Imagine the full intent of the government of Canada running the grease-racks of this nation, intending to be a gasoline jockey. It is another example of an exorbitant imagination run wild with the taxpayers' purse. What they should be doing is giving incentives to the search for new sources of hydrocarbon energy. While that is necessary in this country, they established a company called PetroCan which has the capacity to go all the way to the street level, setting up service stations called PetroCanada.
We now have the potential of government-owned gasoline stations operating the corner gasoline service bars. The simple question is often put: Will gasoline stations now be run like the Post Office? The fundamental question has to be: Does the government, by the very nature of its claim of motivation, have the capacity to be able to operate something in an efficient and jurisprudent manner? When the government thinks up a new airport, it in fact thinks up a new debt. Pickering ran up a $110 million debt and ran it through the paper-shredder. We look at Mirabel and Pickering airports which are, respectively, 88,000 and 18,000 acres of prime agricultural land that have been destroyed in this country. This is simply because of a lack of foresight by those in the transportation department who plan the airport sites. I cannot pass by that comment without mentioning that virtually all across Canada, wherever an airport has been set down it has destroyed large tracts of agricultural land. The airport in Edmonton, Alberta, is built on some of this country's highest quality soil.
As a smaller example, but a very important one, for the satellite airport north of Edmonton, at Villeneuve, there were three sites chosen as being acceptable. They narrowed the three sites down to two. In one of the remaining two they noted that the 4,145 acres recommended for the airport site was on class five and class six soil. I might add that class six soil implies non-improvable, permanent pasture. The other was 45 per cent class one and 50 percent class two soil. In other words the finest classes of soil that we have in this country. The only difference was that one site, the one with the better class soil, was three miles closer to the city. As can be imagined, the Department of Transport, in its wisdom, opted for the site with the highest quality soil, regardless of the fact that Canada today is a net importer of food, coupled with the fact that there are only two sources of food in this world, soil and water. It should be pointed out that today in Canada we are very rapidly destroying our agricultural land. One of the prime sources of that is airport development, industrial development, much of which is linked to transport systems, and certainly airports and airport byways.
The highest growth rate of Air Canada has to be its debt load. If you look at an analysis of the statistics on various bits of information that come out of Air Canada, you will see that nothing in recent years has had a higher percentage increase than the debt and debt interest load of that particular business. We have a bill before the House now asking us to free the debt charges and to put Air Canada under more direct control of the Department of Transport. We have to question very strongly the wisdom of such a move in view of the past record
May 31, 1977

of this government. Almost any Crown corporation we want to examine shows that the net result is a net loss.
If we compare the Crown corporations with the private sector in not only this country but in the United States and other countries where there are industries of comparable size and capital input, we see that in virtually every case the Crown corporation operates at less profit or-and this is so in the majority of cases-at a net loss. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) something in excess of a year ago told the Canadian people that the market place no longer works. I suspect there is probably some degree of truth in that statement because he has interfered with the rules of the marketplace.
When speaking on Bill C-17, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) said that this bill will allow for more direct government control over Air Canada. Naturally we are not going to have the situation where the marketplace is going to work. The government is moving more and more into direct competition, stealing the routes from the private sector such as CP Air.
I heard the voices of the NDP shouting across the chamber a few moments ago when talking about CP Air. It is true that CP Air did operate at a loss. One of the major reasons was that Air Canada stole the most lucrative routes, leaving the shavings for the private sector. That is the major reason we do not have a profitable airline industry in this country such as we see in the United States.
We have to wonder about how the government can run an airline, when we do not even have the respective efficiency coming from the minister. The Minister of Transport did not mind spending $750,000 a year for private jets "Lang Air" tripping across the nation. This is the same minister who wants to run the whole airline, picking up the debt for the airports, for the airplanes, the whole works.
We note the story in the Montreal Gazette that Canadian Pacific may have to sell its air operation. One of the reasons it may have to sell that air operation I have already alluded to, and that is the fact that by the very way in which the Transport Commission in this country establishes air routes it is a known fact to any one who has investigated this situation that CP Air does not operate on the same kind of lucrative routes as Air Canada. If anyone doubts that, I challenge them to travel the triangle from Montreal to Toronto to Ottawa and note that virtually every time you board a plane those planes are running at full capacity.
If any other private sector airline were to operate at such a lucrative capacity in such a lucrative region, they would turn an enormous profit. Yet in that very region just a year ago Air Canada lost $19 million of the taxpayers' money. It goes back to a comparison between Air Canada and Northwest Airlines, two airlines of similar size, and what do we see? On the one hand we see a private sector airline operating at a $100 million profit, and Air Canada operating at a $20 million deficit. That is the kind of difference we have because in Canada the distinguishing fact is that Air Canada has double the staff. That is the nature of the public service. The public service has
Air Canada
a tendency to have a malignant growth upon itself. As a new person develops a new idea, it requires another person to develop the idea, who in turn develops a new idea. The first thing you know, you have a staff out of control. That is true of the whole bureaucracy here in Ottawa; we have witnessed in the past eight to ten years something like a 360 per cent increase in federal government expenditures for the staffing of the public service.
I concede that part of the reason for loss is that we have had some major increases in fuel costs. But that does not take away from the fact that there are airlines companies in the world with the same increases in fuel costs which are operating at a profit. I think what it does point out, however, is that if fuel costs is one of the excuses Air Canada is going to use for its loss situation, then one of the things the government ought to be doing now is coming forward with a program for the discovery of new sources of energy so that we do not have to have the high debt overload on transportation. The other fact that should have been woven into this whole scheme of things is that the government, in its lack of wisdom, chose to toss out support for urban transportation, something that had it gone ahead with in its 1974 election promise to such cities as Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal and other major cities, there would have been a great step forward in terms of fuel economy and fuel saving. In the long run, this would have left more hydrocarbon fuel available for those instruments of transportation that in fact require that kind of fuel, such as airlines and so forth.
Air Canada, then, we see, has twice the staff of its counterpart airlines. While we have used the one example of Northwest Airlines, a similar comparison could be made with numerous other airlines throughout the world. I would simply say that if Orville and Wilbur Wright were here, they certainly would be aghast to see what is happening to the airline industry, noticing that it has been requested to go under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Transport which really, in its lack of wisdom, has not had the capacity to manage anything and show an operational profit.
In conclusion, I think the one thing we can say about Bill C-17 is that its only sure guarantee is that there is going to be an ever-increasing tax burden upon the Canadian public for flight services in this country, because it is not going to be possible to operate an airline to demonstrate efficiency as long as it comes under the direction of governor in council kind of direction, because it will have a lack of direction in its policies, and I think the government is moving in precisely the opposite direction to where it ought to be going. It is diametrically opposed to what it ought to be doing. Air Canada was previously under the jurisdiction of the CNR and, if anything, what it ought to have been told to do was to get even a step further remote from government and to demonstrate it could operate its lines at an efficient cost.
That does not mean, of course, for a single moment, should someone on the other side intend to respond by saying that would mean that certain communities are not serviced, because we know that previously there have been airlines in

May 31, 1977
Air Canada
Canada, not Air Canada, servicing Frobisher Bay and all parts of the Arctic. These have been privately-owned airlines. More recently, while PWA has been taken over by the province of Alberta, the fact remains that that airline operates very much on business principles, is much more remote from government itself and has in fact demonstrated, and continues to demonstrate, that it is an airline which can operate at a profit.
Air Canada, it is now being suggested, should come under the direct thumb of government, and all we are about to witness is a guaranteed loss of taxpayers' funds because the whole modus of government is different from that of the private sector. It is just another example of running at full speed 180 degrees in the opposite direction to what a sensible policy should have been. The government will not, in the years to come, be able to look back and show any kind of benefit at all from this most unfortunate bill which has been placed before the Commons.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to participate in the second reading debate on Bill C-17, the Air Canada Act. It is most appropriate that at long last we should have before us a bill dealing specifically with Air Canada, particularly in view of the fact that this, I gather, is the fortieth anniversary of the creation of Air Canada. So it is a sort of birthday present, in a sense, to Air Canada or to the taxpayers of Canada; I am not sure which.
When I had birthdays years ago, before I stopped counting them, there was always a glorious cake with icing and, sometimes, little tokens in the cake. Sometimes you bit your teeth on them, but you hoped to get a token or a trinket. In view of the fact that we are debating this bill today under the rule which restricts the length of speeches and, ironically, at a time when the Transport Committee is on tour in Atlantic Canada dealing particularly with ports in Atlantic Canada, it may not be possible to get far below the frosting on the cake to see what the trinkets and tokens are in the cake until the measure goes to committee.
I understand there is some disposition to move this bill on to committee, and I also understand from my hon. friend from Battle River (Mr. Malone) that the minister earlier, vaguely in public but perhaps more substantively in private, gave some assurances that amendments will be made in committee which hopefully will take care of some of the objections raised to this bill.
Bill C-17 represents really the first fundamental change in the structure of Air Canada since 1937. Perhaps more relevant than this is the fact that the officials of Air Canada have not
appeared before the transportation committee since 1973, which is another reason why this bill should move quickly into committee. Many matters should be ventilated. We are all aware of the recent royal commission on the financial arrangements of Air Canada and the report of Judge Estey, which raises many questions which have to be answered and which this bill fails to answer. In fact, in some areas the bill seems almost to avoid definite recommendations made by Judge Estey.
As many have said, this is the fortieth anniversary of Air Canada, the national flagship of this country. In the past. Air Canada has earned in a most objective way more praise and kudos than any objective observer can claim it earns today. A few years ago, when I was almost knee high to a grasshopper, I heard it said that Trans-Canada Airlines, as it was then, was one of the best airlines in the air but often was the despair of those on the ground in regard to personnel relations and service. For example, it was said you could not get information from the airline, and there were many other areas of customer and personnel discontent. Its safety record has been one of the best in the world. Any debate about Air Canada either in the House or in committee must acknowledge that tremendous credit is due and tribute should be paid to the professionals in Air Canada who have maintained this fantastically high safety record which, as I say, compares most favourably with that of any other airline.
Perhaps one of the dangers I see in the bill is that it almost contradicts some of the recommendations made by Judge Estey to alter the structure of Air Canada so as to make it more independent and more professional. As others have said, rather than make Air Canada more professional this bill potentially could make it more political. I do not think any hon. member would agree that the professionalism of Air Canada should be subordinated to political matters which could affect adversely the enviable record of professionalism which Air Canada has in the air.
1 am not going into some of the topical questions which have to be debated and assessed. I am not going to talk about control of Air Canada, a matter which this House will eventually have to deal with. 1 am talking about the very structure of Air Canada in terms of its management and administration. One can trace on a graph just what happened when the present government changed the administrative structure of Air Canada. Although we were very conscious of the bicultural nature of Canada, almost out of the blue the government decided to appoint not only a chairman of the board but a president-executive officer of the company. Prior thereto one officer, in effect, directed the affairs of Air Canada. Although there must always be ministerial responsibility in terms of definition of national policy, he was the person to whom we looked to run Air Canada, just as we knew who was running Canadian Pacific. Today Air Canada is one of the major corporations in the country.
As I say, only a few years ago Air Canada's structure was changed and two executive offices were created. I would suggest-and I do so objectively-that some of the problems

May 31, 1977

of morale and confusion in transmitting directions to those further down the totem pole can be traced to those appointments, let alone some of the events which occurred afterwards when there was almost a housecleaning among a lot of competent senior officers in Air Canada, in the result, a whole pyramid of vice-presidents of this and vice-presidents of that was created which diluted the central executive command which theretofore had pretty well been under the control of one man who ran a corporation Canadians were proud of.
Looking at Bill C-17, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that we are now compounding the problem. Instead of having just the chairman of the board-whatever his duties will be, frankly, is somewhat vague-and/or the president-executive officer of the company, whatever his duties may be, it is clear from the bill that you are adding a third party, the governor in council, who is really the minister.
You and I, Mr. Speaker, and other members of the chamber are not that far removed from the period when a few years ago the United Nations tried to change its structure. At that time a fellow called Khrushchev came from Moscow, banged his shoe on the table and wanted to create a troika. He thought that was the way the United Nations should be run so as to represent the people of the world. Instead of one executive officer of the United Nations, the secretary-general, he suggested a troika.
I am apprehensive that under this bill, in the absence of any definition or amendment, in effect there will be a troika consisting of the chairman of the board, the president-executive officer, and the minister who could very well give directions as to the day to day operation of the airline. I think that this would be a retrograde step. I do not want to deal in personalities, and the minister has certainly shown expertise in the use of aircraft. However, I do not think there is any member on either side who has the expertise or competence to start meddling, even indirectly, in the day to day operations of the airline.
This underlines what occurred a few years ago when the government appointed the two officers to whom I have referred. Up until that time Air Canada had been headed by one officer. We are now adding a third in the form of the minister. Although three horses draw sleds in the steppes of Russia, I do not think in organizations troikas have ever worked effectively, certainly not in a complex and complicated undertaking like the national airline of Canada. 1 am hoping that either in this debate or in committee the minister will give an indication of the kinds of amendments he intends to move so that my apprehensions about this three-headed monster will be removed. The cabinet, in terms of national policies, directives and roles, obviously has to give direction. Almost in any bill there is power for the governor in council to define national goals to which any Crown corporation should adhere.
In its present form, this bill takes Air Canada away from the umbrella of the railways. It is a healthy step toward giving it some identity of its own in a structural way and in a
Air Canada
legislative way, but I seriously question removing it from the over-all umbrella of Canadian National and its legislation. In effect, it is being set up as a true Crown corporation and you are not giving it the independence and confidence which the Glassco commission recommended. In effect, you are not giving it the independence and the confidence which Judge Estey recently said the board of directors of Air Canada should have. It is being put into cabinet and right on the minister's table. That is a retrograde step which has to be corrected, as far as I am concerned. I mentioned the troika in terms of executive control. It is a fundamental contradiction when you have three people with executive control. Executive control is non-existent in that situation; you have executive confusion or you have executive dilution to the point where there is no direction. Every person in Air Canada, from the lowest generic flight attendant to the top of the totem pole, wants direction from the executive officer and wants a structure which those persons know who are running Air Canada.
I will not continue ad infinitum, because this House will be debating Bill C-33, the bill amending the National Transportation Act, as well as Bill C-43, the bill amending the communications legislation. I will not repeat here what is obviously going to be said ad infinitum at that time. Under the MacLean commission on transportation in 1903, the railway rates commission was established. At that time it said that transportation and the railways were getting a little too complicated and complex. It recommended that railway rates had to be removed from the variable, unstable atmosphere of the politician who comes and goes at election time or in terms of cabinet ministers. At this time that is obvious in the present cabinet, where ministers come and go in terms of cabinet shuffles. In other words, a minister is giving directions on a day to day basis in terms of something as complex as Air Canada; then comes a cabinet shuffle and he changes to another portfolio; his executive assistant changes to another portfolio, and invariably the deputy minister changes after one or two years. That is no way to run a railway or an airline.
Judge Estey said, in more legalistic terms than I am prepared to do, that Air Canada's board of directors is long overdue and it is just a politicial plum handed out to friends of the party in power. This was also said by the Glassco commission. Judge Estey also said that the directors should have their duties defined and should be appointed for fixed terms under statute, so that they could not be removed by an angry government which did not like what they decided. He also said that they should have some prescribed qualifications because it is a very complicated and complex business. One only has to read the stock pages of the newspapers to realize airlines in the private sector, let alone airlines in the public sector, are having to hustle for every client dollar. Yet they do not have effective hustling because their boards of directors are appointed in the same manner as in Sir John A. Macdonald's days. It is just a ministerial or cabinet plum, with no relationship whatsoever to knowledge or expertise in any facet of transportation, let alone any facet of the airline industry. I am not in a position to make many comments about the red chamber, but as far as I am

concerned there is no way I want the board of directors to be another form of the Senate under this bill, whereby political considerations outweigh any other consideration in those types of appointments.
The hon. member who just spoke before me mentioned the debt structure of Air Canada which is higher than any other airline. I know the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) will be making a few comments later in the debate about the auditing practices and the financial situation of Air Canada. Through persistent questions of his in this House, the government was forced to appoint a royal commission, the Estey commission, to assess and define some of the financial and audit arrangements of Air Canada.
I do not have to waste time now speaking about the freedom of information and the paradox of Crown corporations being financed by taxpayers' money. A member of parliament has difficulty getting information on any phase of the operation, but any member of the public can get that information at a Canadian Transport Commission hearing. If it had not been for the persistent questioning of a fellow by the name of Andrew Roman at the Canadian Transport Commission hearings on the 1974 annual report of Air Canada, none of us would have known.
The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) put questions on the order paper to find out the breakdown of the $20 million deficit of Air Canada in 1974. He was answered by the minister to the effect that that information could not be disclosed because it had a proprietary interest, and since other airlines did not have to disclose such information this would put Air Canada in an adverse position and poor Air Canada would not be able to compete. That was, in effect, the answer that was given.

The words were along those lines, ad infinitum, ad nauseam. As my hon. friend says, that was a shameful answer from the then minister. I am not sure which minister it was because they have been playing musical chairs and ring around the rosey so much. Of course, the next game of musical chairs will occur in July, when this minister will most likely be shunted out. I do not know whether he will be given a wheat bin to sit in, but 1 am prepared to prognosticate that there will be a new minister of transport. 1 have the greatest personal admiration for the present Minister of Transport in terms of ministerial responsibility.
I heard some of the strange announcements by the minister the other day when he was making policy statements in the deep east. This was at a time when a parliamentary committee there was studying transport, when the CTC was studying transport and when the Sullivan commission was studying transport in all of Atlantic Canada. Suddenly out of the blue, like pulling tablets out of the sky, this minister, from on high, makes policy statements which sound fairly interesting until they are really looked at. In terms of information, I cannot see why a member of parliament cannot get what the commission-

ers will tell counsel before the Canadian Transport Commission by putting a proper question on the order paper.
That is how we found out that $19 million of the $20 million Air Canada lost in 1974 was lost between Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto. One might think that is the most lucrative run in Canada. A further breakdown of the figures showed that on the prairies Air Canada made a profit of $20 million. This examination took place before the Canadian Transport Commission; this knowledge did not become known through answers in this House or before the committee. Even in the Atlantic area, which is supposed to be a depressed area, Air Canada broke even. The $19 million loss occurred right here in the heartland between Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto. Thank goodness we had a persistent counsel before the commission hearings who got that information. That was an insult to parliament. The minister should never have signed the order saying that that information was not to be given to the hon. member for Vegreville.
I know my time is running out quickly because of the rule which shortens the time for speeches in order to expedite the business so that we can get this log jam over with and so that we might have some type of summer recess before different activities begin in the fall. I would like to talk very briefly about Air Canada and Atlantic Canada. Just because we produce sardines in Atlantic Canada, I do not understand why we should be treated like sardines when it comes to Air service. 1 refer to trips from Atlantic Canada to upper Canada and to the west.
1 do not have the figures for this year or last year, but I think it was three years ago in the committee-without divulging cost figures-I was informed by officials of Air Canada that in Atlantic Canada, and I can understand this because of our geographic location, there was a higher density of passengers per air mile than in any other region of Canada because, frankly, more and more people were taking Air Canada. That was the only airline which effectively connected with upper Canada until Eastern Provincial Airlines started to give service into Montreal. However, if you want to go to Toronto, Ottawa or further west, you have to use Air Canada.
I cannot fly from Halifax to upper Canada without being jammed into a DC-9 for almost every flight. They land in Montreal before they get down to day to day operations. I was accusing the minister of perhaps not getting involved in day to day operations. As a member of parliament, 1 do not mind bringing up some of the practical problems which I as a member of the consuming, flying public, as well as thousands of others have experienced.
To me it is a complete paradox that we fly from Halifax in a DC-9 which is jammed tighter than any sardine can from Blacks Harbour. Blacks Harbour is where sardines are canned. People are shovelled and shoe-horned into these DC-9s, and they fly to Montreal, if that is the way they are connecting to another flight westward. They fly to Montreal, but they do not
May 31, 1977

land anywhere close to the terminal. They always land at the international section, gates 48, 49, 50, 51 or 52.

I know that the minister from Prince Edward Island has gone through this, as 1 have. To connect to Ottawa you have to trundle off from the international gate-I forget where the numbers start, but it could be anywhere from gate 46 to gate 56-and you get on the conveyor belt and go all the way to gates 1, 2 or 3. 1 do not think Air Canada cares. It is ironic that as you stumble off the conveyor belt and go up two flights of stairs to get to the terminal so that you can get back to gate 6, you walk by something called Express Air, and you wonder whether there really is something fast in this system. Express Air travels between Montreal and Toronto on the hour, every hour. You look out and see a DC-9. Anything bigger would not be needed on the hour, every hour after rush hour. Surely it is not that busy. You also see a stretched DC-8 sitting there. I have been on a stretched DC-8 when there have been 10, 20 or 30 passengers, at most, expressing from Montreal to Toronto or from Toronto to Montreal on that fast, vital service. That is one of the reasons $19 million of the $20 million deficit of 1974 was created by Air Canada while other parts of the country did not even receive minimum service. I have a long frame, and sometimes 1 can tuck into a DC-9 seat, but I do not see why we could not have more DC-8s. That would help. More scheduling is also needed.
I must, however, give Air Canada credit because fortunately there is now-at least in the off-season-one regular flight from Ottawa to Halifax, and vice versa. In the summer season there are two flights, and I cannot complain about that. I appreciate it very much and I know other people who fly quite a bit also appreciate it. However, this business of always flying the DC-9 and this problem with regard to the landing positions in Montreal could mean that many passengers will try to avoid Montreal like the plague. These things could be corrected with a few little administrative changes. As I say, just because we produce sardines, Air Canada seems to think we should be treated like sardines and I think that is too bad.
Air Canada
There are many other things that could be said about Air Canada. I could refer to the allocation of routes. Perhaps this bill will have some effect in that regard. The minister is from the west, and he is a man who makes speeches about the west from time to time. I would like to be fair to him, but I would like to have a look at the chronology of the last allocation. I think Senator Marchand was the minister at the time. The last allocation of routes between Air Canada and CP Air was based on one thing in terms of objectives in the communications industry, and that was to make sure CP Air would start to have deficits. There are many things which could be said about that.
I forget the numbers, but what happened to Air Canada when it got the plums is very graphic. CP Air got very few, and even the plums CP Air had were cut into by the alternative routes which were given to Air Canada. This cut into the markets which prior to that had been CP Air markets. I am sure some hon. members of the House will not agree, but I think it was a very progressive step-and I would like to see it extended in Atlantic Canada-when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the minister of transport of those days used some imagination and initiative and extended CP Air into many areas of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I will cut through all the other things I could have said. I appreciate the good manners of the House and I will not abuse this privilege. I have not been overly critical or political today. The minister knows that. But I would like to summarize what has happened to Air Canada compared with CP Air. I hope this bill will start to correct the situation. In the most basic human terms, I ask the minister perhaps some day to avoid taking a special plane and to get on the morning plane from Ottawa to Toronto. I am referring to the 7.10 a.m. or 7.20 a.m. flight. If the minister flies Air Canada he will get an expanded continental breakfast. He will get a little more than a soggy, heavy croissant. He will get rice crispies or perhaps cornflakes in a plastic cup, and sometimes there are two or three grapes. You get a little cup of juice and cornflakes with three grapes. What dietetic emancipation and imagination there is in some kitchen, putting in those three grapes! They must have an agreement with Caesar Chavez of California to help the grape industry. That is the only explanation I can find for the addition of those two or three hormones of fruit. You have the small cup of juice juice, cornflakes with the three grapes, and then the stewardess comes by and pours coffee and tea.
I cannot explain the reason for the difference, but when you fly by CP Air on the morning flight at about the same time- and the plane is full as anyone who has taken the flight
80016-45V2

May 31, 1977
Air Canada
knows-you get a full breakfast, as good a breakfast as you would get in any hotel. You get juice, fresh fruit, scrambled eggs, bacon, sausage, and tea or coffee. You have the whole thing.
I should like to conclude with some generalities with which 1 opened my comments. Years ago, and still today, fortunately, Air Canada has been and is recognized as one of the best airlines from the point of view of air safety and air service, but ever since the change took place in the executive command of Air Canada three or four years ago, when they appointed two officers to reflect the bilingual duality of the land, a chairman of the board and an executive officer, the service to people on the ground has deteriorated. I am most apprehensive that when we add the third element, which this bill does, in effect, by giving direct cabinet control in the day to day operations, thus creating a troika, service will go down further.
Let me say, in conclusion, that this would perhaps be a precedent and I do not know how the minister would respond to it-frankly, I do not know whether there is a statutory prohibition-but we just had the Estey royal commission, the report of which was filed when this bill was introduced not too long ago. This bill was given first reading in October, 1976. The taxpayers paid for the royal commission which came up with a very good and objective report. Of course, the written word does convey certain things, but it seems to me that if we are to come up with the best form, organization and structure for Air Canada, perhaps the minister, the House and the committee when it is dealing with the bill should consider seriously calling in Judge Estey. He was a commissioner, now he is a judicial officer. He has made his report, and frankly I think that that study could give us a much better charter for Air Canada than does Bill C-17 at present.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow on the comments of the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan). I am sure we will all discover as the day goes on that many maritime members of parliament will want to participate in this debate because of the deep concern they all have over the deteriorating service that is presently made available to people in Atlantic Canada by Air Canada which is the base commercial airline available to our area and, unfortunately, because of government decision, the only airline that is available to our area to move our people between the Atlantic region and the rest of the nation. I have been having a running battle with officials of Air Canada in Altantic Canada over the rotten service-it could not be described in any other way-that is presently available to the patrons of that airline in our part of Canada.
Today, from the closest air terminal to my constituency in Moncton you either have to get up in the middle of the night in order to get to Ottawa or, if you do not take that flight or cannot get on it, you have to wait until the middle of the night again in order to catch another plane that will move you to this part of the country. 1 live some 40 miles from Moncton. The morning flight to Montreal and Ottawa leaves at 7.15 a.m., which means that in Amherst I have to get up at 5.30 in the morning in order to catch the plane. If I do not want to take

that flight, then I have to wait until 7.20 p.m., a full 12 hours, before I can get another flight. If I have to come to Ottawa, I leave Moncton at 7.20 p.m., which is 6.20 p.m. Ottawa time, and I do not arrive in Ottawa until 10.30 p.m. If I am lucky and the connections are as they are supposed to be, I do not get into the kind of mix-up that I seem to experience every time I try to make the connection from Montreal to Ottawa.
It is nothing short of scandalous. It is the worst service that I can recall being made available to our area by Air Canada in any schedule, and especially during the summer months when there is the greatest demand for seats on the airline. I cannot imagine how Air Canada can co-ordinate its present flight schedule with the extra demand from people who want to go to the Maritimes at least in the summer time to enjoy the recreational facilities we have available to all Canadians which are second to none in North America. Yet Air Canada does absolutely nothing to give any kind of service that would assist in any way the tourist industry in our part of Canada which is so vital to our over-all economic prospects for the future.
There seems to be some kind of syndrome in the Air Canada head office which determines that schedules for Atlantic Canada are like the tail on the donkey. You pin it on after you have prepared timetables for everywhere else to everybody else's satisfaction. It is almost like the case of blind-man's-buff. You never know now where the tail will be pinned or what kinds of atrocities they will commit against the travelling public which happens to be located in Atlantic Canada either permanently or as travellers.
I do not understand the philosophy of Air Canada nor the government's philosophy. If we are to assist in overcoming regional economic disparity, then surely we must develop a system which will make it easier for our businessmen to move between Atlantic Canada and the central region of this country as well as other parts of the country. Yet they put every kind of roadblock in our way in getting our businessmen out of the region and other businessmen into the region. Therefore, the degree of frustration toward Air Canada, and indirectly toward the government, that results from this is hard to imagine unless you happen to live in Atlantic Canada and have to put up with the inconveniences that seem almost like a conspiracy against our area so far as air travel is concerned.
A few years ago I attended commission hearings at which Canadian Pacific made an effort to try to secure a line between eastern Toronto and Halifax or Montreal and Halifax to give some competition to Air Canada. Unfortunately, this was denied. I say "unfortunately" because what happened as a result of Canadian Pacific Airlines being denied even one flight into and out of the region was that Air Canada was given virtually a monopoly to do what it wanted, whether we liked it or not. Every time a complaint is made we get a put down from the airlines as a response. In effect, they are saying, "You take what we give you, like it or not. We could not care less, because we are in command. You are going to fly with us or not fly at all."
May 31, 1977

The only half decent service that is available to the Atlantic provinces is provided by Eastern Provincial Airways, but unfortunately the schedules they are forced to use make you feel like a yo-yo: you go up and down all the time. They do not even have time to serve tea or coffee. Direct routing between the Atlantic provinces and Montreal has been denied the airline. At the same time, Air Canada incurs multi-million dollar deficits which it uses as an excuse for not allowing any other airline to compete. So we have to put up with EPA, with its up and down schedule, or with Air Canada that only flies in the middle of the night, between midnight and 7 a.m. or between 7 p.m. and midnight. Nothing happens through the day at all. That is a terrible schedule to inflict upon an area. It makes me wonder what the employees of Air Canada do. In Moncton, for instance, there is nothing to do between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. because there are no flights.
I must say, however, that the Air Canada employees give every assistance with the flights that are available. I have nothing but good to say of my contacts with them. Their public relations are very good because they really have nothing to sell. They have learned how to say no very nicely. I must also give credit to Air Canada for their baggage handling. I have seldom encountered a problem in this respect when travelling with Air Canada, which is amazing when you consider the amount of baggage that is moved. I think they deserve special commendation for the efficient way they do the job.
I must say, however, that it is significant that in Atlantic Canada we are the last to get new planes. I have not seen anything but a DC-9 for so long that I wonder if Air Canada has any other kind of aircraft. Atlantic Canada suffers from the central Canada syndrome that the best must be used between Montreal and Toronto, and nowhere else. The L-1011 was used for a little while in the area, but suddenly it was removed and the DC-9 put back in service. Sometimes 1 wonder that they do not send us back to the Viscount. Everything else in Air Canada's service has gone backwards in our area, so we will probably end up with aircraft that are in mothballs at the moment.
I would like to remind the minister that there is no time like the present to make Canadians feel it is worth-while to be part of this country, but so long as Air Canada provides the kind of service we have at present we will always feel neglected. It is only after everyone else is served that we can hope for improvement. Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that the air terminal at Charlottetown must be the worst in Canada. For a long time there has been talk of a new terminal, but nothing has happened. It is nothing short of a national scandal that one of our provincial capitals has such a lousy airport. But that is the kind of treatment we have come to expect.
It is hard to believe that the government is serious about ever providing us with something that is comparable to the rest of the country. We face a tourist season, but we still have terrible schedules and a rundown terminal. I would ask the minister to do something to improve conditions and provide us
Air Canada
with a schedule as good as that in any other part of the country. The present one is the worst we have had for 20 years. We are almost back to the days of Lindbergh. It is time the government stepped in and told Air Canada to provide Atlantic Canada with air service comparable to what is available in other parts of the country.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to speeches made in this debate and have read, as well, what my colleagues said in this House. The government is bringing forward a constructive measure, in principle. Many of the things I want to say have already been said by others, perhaps better than I can say them. However, 1 was troubled about the government's delay in bringing this legislation forward.
Now that the Bill C-17 is before the House, neither I nor my party intend to delay passage to committee. It seems to me that Parliament has already wasted a number of years. The former minister of transport who is now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), said in March, 1972 that we needed this legislation. Since then much has happened in the country and to Air Canada, but it is good to see this bill at last dealing with some of the questions which in the opinion of members of parliament ought to be dealt with. The need to deal with them has been apparent for a number of years.
When 1 first read the bill I was impressed with it and thought that it incorporated many of Chief Justice Estey's recommendations. But the number of references to the governor in council concerned me. It seemed to me that the bill would give the minister power to wield an inordinate amount of control, perhaps at the expense of the airline's management. I was reassured to hear the minister say that at some later stage, as a result of discussions, amendments will be introduced which will qualify the text of the bill as it now reads. He was speaking of that part of the bill providing for the giving of directions. According to the minister, as he is reported in Hansard, the directions to be given by the governor in council will be directions of a general nature. He went on to say that it is not the intention or purpose of the government to give direction in relation to the day to day operation of the airline. If the minister meant what he said and his words can be translated into proper amendments in committee, many of the concerns of members of parliament on this point, particularly in my party, will be laid to rest.
In the past, Air Canada has been one of our better Crown corporations. Only in the fairly recent past, when people with non-airline or non-transport experience were appointed to senior positions in the airline, have some of the airline's difficulties become apparent. Many of those difficulties are now in the process of being eliminated. As my colleague from Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates) noted, no corporation, Crown or otherwise, has a more dedicated and capable work force than Air Canada. Given good, sound financial direction and a minimum of government interference, I think Air Canada can again reach the heights of efficiency and

May 31, 1977
Air Canada
goodwill it enjoyed a few years ago. In my opinion, it is on its way to regaining its former position.
Many constructive suggestions have been conveyed to the minister by Air Canada, members of parliament, and 1 hope from other sources. I should like to deal positively now, with some points which I am sure the minister has heard before. Nevertheless, I think they should be put on record. Also, since I will not neglect the negative side of the bill in my remarks, I shall make some suggestions for improvement. I shall also deal with one activity in which Air Canada has participated and for which it ought to be condemned. I refer to the company's involvement with the de-icing facilities at Mirabel. I shall come to that later.
The minister said in his speech last week, as reported in Hansard, that he feels it is his responsibility to achieve the maximum possible efficiency in all aspects of the airline's operation. I think the minister would also agree that if possible Air Canada's profitability ought to be kept in the forefront. The airline has always striven to make a profit if that was possible. Only in recent years has it begun to show an alarming pattern of operating deficits. Personally, I should like to see an express provision in the bill saying that the government intends Air Canada to be profitable. That would be consistent with the minister's statements and would be valuable in boosting employee morale.
Such a provision would also give potential investors the confidence of knowing the company is commercially oriented. This point is important, since this bill deals with changes to the company's capital structure. I should like to see some language inserted, perhaps in the preamble or in clause 6, in that clause under the title "Capacities and activities of the corporation", spelling out tersely but explicitly some definite commitment for making the airline a profitable operation.
It is obvious, from a reading of the bill, that the airline may engage in a number of activities which are over and above its paramount purpose. I think some definitions in this respect could be improved in committee. Those activities not listed by implication are prohibited. Perhaps we should examine the legislation carefully and see if we cannot indicate with more precision exactly what Air Canada can and should do. I do not think for example, we should give it carte blanche to do anything it wants or compete unfairly with other like enterprises in the private sector.
I mentioned earlier the matter of directions. The bill says that the corporation shall comply with direction given to it in writing by the governor in council. Such directions are unqualified. Since the minister mentioned them in his speech, I think one can assume he is well aware that, taken literally, such language would enable the government to interfere in the day to day operations of Air Canada. I understand the Air Canada management thinks the government ought to confine itself to policy direction. Obviously, Chief Justice Estey had this in mind when he raised the point in his report, and 1 agree.
I now raise the question of Air Canada service. Obviously, for various reasons in the past Air Canada has been directed to provide service on routes which no private airline could have

flown profitably. Clearly, clause 9 empowers the government to compensate Air Canada for losses arising from the provision of that type of uneconomic service. I believe the committee should consider making such compensation mandatory. Such language should be spelled out in the act clearly, in order to show management, the public and employees of Air Canada that the airline shall not suffer financially as a result of such direction to provide unprofitable services to remote areas domestically or internationally.
I also believe that the method of calculating such losses ought to be in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. Some procedures should be spelled out, so that the department itself will not have power to say how large the losses are. If there is any dispute, the matter ought to go to some sort of arbitration procedure.
We are now considering a different type of capital debt structure for the company. In order to ensure that Air Canada can market its future securities at the lowest possible rate of interest, in order to attract potential investors and encourage investment, I suggest the bill should be amended to make Air Canada securities a legal and eligible investment from any point of view. Certain Canadian companies such as insurance and trust companies may not, under the legislation governing them, invest their funds in the securities of another company unless the latter meets certain tests specified in the governing legislation qualifying it as a "legal for life" investment. That is a term in use in the investment world. It seems to me that the committee ought to consider this point when considering.
The borrowing power of Air Canada is covered in clause 15 of this bill. This power becomes immensely important when you consider that only a few years ago, at the end of the war, you could buy a pretty good aircraft for passenger service for around $1 million. Today's wide-bodied jets cost $30 million or $40 million together with spare parts. The financing of these very important and necessary showcases of Air Canada's fleet is a major undertaking and it is much more complicated than it used to be.
The bill provides that the approval of the Minister of Finance must be obtained before the corporation can borrow any money. This is not entirely necessary nor desirable from Air Canada's point of view. It extends the government's control too far into the day to day operations of the airline and its management. In other words, the corporation's financial plans, including the need to raise funds externally, would be apparent in its annual budget which requires approval by order in council on the joint recommendation of the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Finance, and the President of Treasury Board. If the budget and resulting external financing requirements are approved, further government approvals related to implementing such plans introduce what any company would believe to be overcontrol by the government, detrimental to the effective and efficient implementation of approved plans by the management.
May 31, 1977

Approval of long-term financing action is a normal prerogative of a corporation's board of directors. It should not be through unnecessary, complicated scrutiny by people who in the normal course of events would not find it necessary to do this with other corporations of Air Canada's stature, as is the case with our national air carrier. The need for government approval of post-budget action and decisions covering unspecified terms would adversely affect the company's flexibility. I hope the minister will be receptive to taking a look at this in committee as well.
There have been a lot of problems in the past with Air Canada's auditing. Without opening old wounds, it is only necessary to remind the House that these complications arose because of arbitrary action taken by the government which did not meet good business principles and were not satisfactory under the circumstances. This bill which indicates that auditors will be appointed annually by the governor in council should be modified so that management of the corporation will be consulted. There was a totally unnecessary occasion of embarrassment to the airline in the past when we had the ridiculous situation of three sets of auditors-one going, one coming, and one in the process of leaving. We do not want to get into that sort of era again.
The bill requires an audit to be done of the accounts and financial transactions of the corporation and requires that the auditors report on same to the minister. As is the case in the private sector and under general corporate law, the board of directors of Air Canada should be entitled to an audit report on the company's financial statements and affairs before it approves the accounts and financial transactions for the fiscal year. Again, there ought to be more consultation and more options available to management. Just because Air Canada is a Crown corporation is no reason why it should be penalized through the extent of having excessive control exerted over it. On its record, it deserves far more trust and confidence than, for example, AECL. That should be kept in mind.
Clause 18 provides that the governor in council may request reports of any kind at any time as it deems appropriate from the corporation, and the corporation shall comply with any such request. I would suggest that Air Canada must take a pretty dim view of any such proposal. It is unnecessary and could tend to abuse.
Members of parliament must ensure that this airline is not converted, either advertently or inadvertently, into some sort of government agency rather than a normal commercial enterprise under the broad direction of government. Air Canada, on its record, has been one of the great airlines of the world. It is only in recent years, as mentioned before, that it has run into any difficulty. Something we must be careful about in trying to give Air Canada the type of flexibility and capacity it requires is that we do not allow civil servants, who to some extent are going to follow their natural tendencies, to try to exert a type of control that is going to take away from Air Canada's ordinary initiatives.
I would like to talk about the board of directors of Air Canada for a moment. Rather than having the civil servants
Air Canada
lurking in the background, if it is deemed desirable it would be better to have one or two on the board of directors where they can speak out freely and their actions can be assessed and judged-take away that anonymity.
In considering the qualifications of the board of directors it would be very desirable that they have some expertise in transport-related matters or in business. As far as possible, they should be representative of certain areas of the country. When Air Canada is considering factors that are regional, these people can speak with some knowledge and authority of the situation. They will not simply be holding seats based on political or other prerogatives that have earned their being appointed to the position. The minister will be aware of this, and I am sure he will try earnestly to keep this from happening so that Air Canada's board of directors are not redundant or merely holding down their positions because they have earned them in some way that is not related to the type of expertise they are expected to provide.
As an example of something that Air Canada and Transport have collaborated on recently and completely messed up, to show the other side of some of Air Canada's activities, 1 want to talk very briefly about the de-icing facility at Mirabel. This has interested me for some time and the minister and I have had some correspondence about it. The taxpayers of Canada are now the proud owners of a de-icing facility, through the Department of Transport. It cost the taxpayers a lot of money, between $7 million and $10 million, and that may be a low estimate.
Initially, as I understand it, Air Canada decided that it wanted to control this de-icing facility. They felt it would be in the company's best interest to do so. In 1973 the company suddenly came to the realization that it lacked the money and expertise to accomplish this. Transport decided it should step in and provide some assistance. Also, there were people in the private sector who showed an interest in this particular facility, which made Air Canada uneasy.
Air Canada first decided that they wanted it. Second, they felt they could not handle it. They then did an about-face and decided that they, together with people from Transport, would design this de-icing facility at Mirabel. From that point on, things went from bad to worse. Millions of dollars were spent. Committees were formed, at the initiative of Transport and Air Canada, which involved at various times representatives of major air carriers, ATAC, and so on. Proposals were invited and cancelled; tenders were called and cancelled in an irregular way.
This House will recall that questions were asked last year about some of the circumstances under which a de-icing facility, and for some unknown reason the tenders were cancelled at the last moment without proper notice. Allegedly, a telex was sent, but to this date it has never been found. In any event, the first winter's operation was a disaster. The facility was shut down in December and remained closed until well into the new year.

May 31, 1977
Air Canada
On some occasions there were delays due to de-icing for as long as five hours, causing all sorts of complications to major air carriers, and to passengers. KLM had occasion to complain, as did CP. As I understand it, some of the correspondence the minister has probably seen is so hot that it virtually singes the paper, as the airlines detailed some of the incompetence and some of the complications occasioned by this not so fortuitous blending of Air Canada and the Department of Transport.
On May 26 of this year, for example, in an effort to deal with this continuing problem resulting from Air Canada's refusal to permit anyone else but themselves to participate in this de-icing project, and the failure to call tenders, Transport asked the current ATAC committee, which is the second one which has been formed, if they would like to have representatives from IATA attend the meeting, and if my information is correct they were told they did not want representatives of IATA to watch them wash their linen in front of the world in trying to come to some sort of reasonable conclusion to get out of this demonstrable fiasco.
I have mentioned this rather detailed example to illustrate that if Air Canada is to be given increasing authority-and I, for one, feel that they should be given that authority and flexibility-they must not use this increased flexibility and authority to get into areas where they either lack the capacity or other means to compete and do a good job. At the same time, it must be made clear to Air Canada that as a Crown corporation, while they should have every occasion to do those things which facilitate their main object, that is to say, transporting people and participating in enterprises related to transportation, they should not necessarily be allowed to get too far afield, because I think it is pretty clear that even the most efficient Crown corporation has yet to demonstrate that it is a match for a well-managed private corporation which has to sink or swim on its own merits. It should be noted in this connection that the private sector corporations are in a far better position to make a contribution back to the economy in terms of tax dollars, and so on.
1 want to make my feelings clear. Air Canada, despite the increased powers contemplated under the bill, should be watched closely to make certain that it does not expand too rapidly, and in areas such as de-icing where so far it has shown itself to be unqualified to do the job which some other company, maybe General Aviation, maybe some other private company, could have done better. Coming back to the de-icing operation for a moment, I hope the minister will consult with his colleagues in Treasury Board bearing in mind that, as 1 understand the situation, it is government policy that, publicly-owned facilities such as this unit at Mirabel should in every possible sense be open to public tender. This is the only way in which taxpayers are going to be able to decide whether this very expensive de-icing capability which has been bought with their money is a success and can be operated, or whether in the final analysis cement must be poured over it and a new start made.
Coming back to the question of the employees of Air Canada and the labour difficulties which have plagued this company, I should like to see the minister consider whether or not in the process of the capital restructuring of this company it might not be feasible to make provision for some of the employees of Air Canada, and there are many thousands of them, who would wish to invest in their company, to do so. It would be very interesting to see what sort of response the government would get to this type of initiative.
I also think that, just as in the case of civil servants having some legitimate function to perform, it should be out in the open where people can assess their decisions and input, as has been mentioned before, and in the case of this Crown corporation it would be very useful to get a policy input from some of the people who work for the company in technical areas particularly. As far as some of the decisions are concerned which, with the benefit of hindsight, seem less than wise, I believe that if some of the maintenance people of Air Canada and some of the pilots and flight crews had had a consultative role to play, we would not have seen Air Canada buy the L-1011.
I have been told repeatedly by pilots that this is not a well-balanced or particularly satisfying aircraft to operate. It was designed to have a stretched model later on, and as a result it does not fly perfectly level in the air. 1 was told it is very difficult sometimes, as a result, for the stewardesses to serve food on this aircraft because the pilot has, as is often said, to fly it a bit up on the step with the nose elevated one or two degrees in order to compensate for its lack of balance. This information may or may not be sound; I don't know. But when you have an airline like Air Canada with approximately 20,000 employees, many of them highly trained and competent people who are watching closely their competitors and who have to be conversant with the latest types of equipment, the servicing and operations, and the merits of different aircraft, it seems to me a waste that some of their knowledge and capability cannot be utilized in an organized way, perhaps through a representative on the board of directors or on a consultative basis through their unions. Advice from the employees might well help the airline improve the quality of some of its operational decisions.
It is far better for this type of input to be available to Air Canada from its own employees than to have that type of suggestion as to what type of aircraft they should buy, or how they should finance them, made by mandarins in government who have never had the occasion to fly an aircraft or to worry about meeting a payroll or servicing the sort of equipment the airline uses. I hope the minister will consider some sort of innovative approach on this basis.

speechtext: I am informed by the Departments of Regional Economic Expansion, Finance and Industry, Trade and Commerce as follows: (a) See question No. 1346 answered on March 11, 1977. There is, however, a program of general application, the machinery program, which is administered by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The program covers a broad range of machines, as well as their accessories, attachments, control equipment, tools and parts, used by the manufacturing and service industries. It provides for remission of duty on imported machinery when the Machinery and Equipment Advisory Board considers that reasonably equivalent machinery is not available from Canadian production and that remission is in the public interest, (c) The results of enquiries by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce indicate that there are no measures in Ireland which allow full relief from import duties on plant and equipment for industry in designated development areas. The existing custom licensing provisions empower the Minister of Industry and Commerce to waive the custom duties only to the extent that Irish duty is higher than Community Common Tariff (CCT) with regard to plant and equipment not manufactured in Ireland. However, as of July 1, 1977, Ireland will apply CCT fully. subsubtopic: U.S. TARIFFS ON OILSEED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
1.	Does the government plan to press the United States for the removal of its tariffs on flax, linoil and linseed meal?

2.	Has the government pressed for their removal previously and (a) if not, for what reason (b) if so, what has been the US response?

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh Poulin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: U.S. TARIFFS ON OILSEED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
1. Both Canada and the United States are currently participating in multilateral trade negotiations in Geneva aimed at the reduction or elimination of tariff and non-tariff barriers to international trade. The Canadian Trade and Tariffs Committee was established in 1973 to receive the views of all Canadians with respect to Canada's participation in these trade negotiations. Since that time, several Canadian interests, including provincial governments and industry associations, have suggested that Canada should seek reduction or removal of U.S.A. tariffs on certain oilseed products. These include not only flaxseed, linoil and linseed meal, but also certain rapeseed, sunflowerseed and mustardseed products. The Canadian delegation in Geneva has notified the U.S.A. of our export interest in these and other agricultural products, and we will be pursuing this matter in the course of the negotiations.
2.	Under the U.S.A. Trade Act of 1974, the President has been granted the authority to negotiate the removal of U.S.A. tariffs of 5 percent ad valorem or lower. It is therefore possible that complete elimination of the U.S.A. tariffs on flaxseed and on linseed meal might be negotiated. U.S.A. tariffs above 5 percent ad valorem, such as that which applies on linseed oil, would be eligible for a maximum duty reduction of 60 percent.
3.	The current round of multilateral trade negotiations is the first to take place since the Kennedy Round of 1964-67. At the time of the Kennedy Round, Canada, as the principal supplier to the United States of linseed oil cake and meal, was able to successfully negotiate a reduction in the U.S.A. duty from 0.22 cent lb. to the current 0.12 cent lb. As Canada was not a significant supplier of either flaxseed or linoil to the U.S.A., we were not in a position to press for a reduction of U.S.A. duties on those products. Since the Kennedy Round, however, Canada has become the principal foreign supplier of all three products to the U.S.A. market, and we will therefore be in a better position to press our interests in the current trade negotiations.
