speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to listen to the remarks of the previous speaker. He has a great interest in Air Canada, as have many other hon. members. I, too, am concerned that the changes which are being made are not necessarily in the interest of Air Canada but rather are in the interests of civil servants and the government, who want to have more say in the operation of Air Canada. I listened with interest to the charges which were being made about the unwillingness of Air Canada to schedule flights in the maritime provinces at times which would meet the convenience of people travelling into central Canada. While 1 have no particular interest in Air Canada from that point of view, Air Canada having left my part of the country and having left much of northern Ontario and northern Quebec, I still am interested in the development of a national airline which can bring the parts of Canada which are easy to service and unite together with those areas which are not so easy to service.
There seems to be little interest on the part of the national carrier to have schedules which would provide domestic travel service which would be a unifying factor in our country. Second, it seems to me that Air Canada should have on its board of directors those people who run the airline. Others have mentioned this, particularly the previous speaker. As the previous speaker said, it may be necessary to have representatives from the civil service, if it is the intention of the government to allow the civil service to have some say in the running of the airline. If that is the case, some civil servants should be on the board of directors and should take some interest in how the airline is run. There should also be representation on a regional basis.
The airline should be able to do something it has not yet been able to do. It should be able to set up a sales agency to put together package tour arrangements, which Air Canada has totally failed to do up until now. True, Air Canada has been operating Sunflights, but it has never been able to break even. It has never been able to make any money, and it has never understood why it cannot handle tourist traffic to other countries. It is quite likely that if Air Canada were able to get into the tourist field and succeed, it would be able to afford the kind of aircraft it needs and to make better utilization of that aircraft. We can use Quebecair and Nordair as examples. Quebecair and Nordair under no circumstances could afford the type of aircraft they have if they were used only for domestic purposes. They are flying Boeing 727's, Boeing 737's and several other aircraft which they in no way could afford for their domestic travel only. They would not be able to keep up the payments on those aircraft if they depended on their domestic scheduled routes, but they have been able to utilize those aircraft at the weekends. In fact, Nordair flies each aircraft back and forth to the Caribbean four times per weekend. If tourist operators are using those aircraft, they are
Air Canada
likely filled to capacity or near capacity, which would be unlikely on a seven day basis on scheduled flights.
One thing Air Canada has never been able to do is relate its prestige to domestic needs. I am sure the government wants to have prestige aircraft flying the flag of Canada in other countries, and I am surprised at the fragmentation which has taken place in the airline. For years I have travelled Air Canada. Air Canada once went from Montreal to Ottawa, Val d'Or, Rouyn, Earlton, North Bay, Toronto and back to Montreal. It covered half the continent with one aircraft and did a reasonable job. However, that type of schedule will not carry the traffic-if it is operating twice a day-which would warrant the use of DC-9's. In fact, I doubt whether the Viscount was feasible on that run. The Viscount has been phased out. I do not know what happened at the management level of Air Canada, but obviously it should have looked at some of the ancillary areas it was going to service, and it should have provided an aircraft for those areas.
There is nothing wrong with DC-9's. Someone mentioned that he would much rather travel on a DC-8. Well, I suggest he talk to an engineer about the DC-8. He might find that it might not be as attractive to travel on that aircraft as he thinks. We should have a small aircraft, but Air Canada has never purchased one. Presently I travel on a commercial scheduled airline which flies DC-3's. There is nothing wrong with DC-3's. Perhaps new DC-3's should be built. Some of the DC-3's 1 am flying on now have a lifespan which is almost, 1 suppose, as long as my own. Many of them are Second World War aircraft, and they are doing a fairly good job. They are economic on short runs. However, in Ontario we have also had to develop a provincial government airline. I think the fact Air Canada was providing much of the rest of the country with the kind of aircraft which could fly those small scheduled runs had some merit. Air Canada now has a very expensive and normally efficient reservation system which operates by computer, and I think it does a reasonably good job. Most of the small ancillary airlines cannot provide that kind of service unless they are tied in with Air Canada. Recently some did become tied in with Air Canada.
1 fly First Air, which is a commercial operation of Bradley Air Services. Bradley is now flying an Otter between Ottawa and Montreal, to Mirabel. Because Bradley is going into Mirabel with that Otter three times a day, Air Canada is quite happy to put Bradley on the computer. First Air now goes to North Bay and Sudbury, and it is also on the computer system because of the arrangement which was made for Mirabel. It seems to me that the management of Air Canada should have a choice of what to do.
I am not happy about CP getting into the national domestic routes in Canada because I am not sure that 22 million or 23 million people can carry the overhead which is necessary to operate two international companies. Certainly CP and Air Canada are fairly large international airlines, considering the size of our country and the length of the trips those airlines have to make on scheduled runs outside this country. If we go into the international Field, we have to have aircraft which are

May 31, 1977
Air Canada
capable of doing the job. We should also be handling many domestic routes in this country, and they should be either operated in conjuction with Air Canada or in partnership with them. It was suggested some time ago that we buy into Wardair. The reason for that was not that we needed their aircraft. All we needed was Tom Ward's expertise in the field of package tourist operations. I was opposed to our buying it because I was of the opinion that rather them buying it we should take over the operation. In addition, I was frightened of Air Canada getting into any other field than flying airplanes.
This is what happened to the railroads. We allowed CNR to buy and operate hotels, to buy real estate, smelters, truck lines, and so forth. Pretty soon they were making more money out of their subsidiaries than they were out of the railroads, so they quit running the railroads. They did not put any balast on the tracks and they did not fix their running equipment. They were operating railroads on the basis of a little bit for the railroad and a whole lot for the subsidiaries which were more valuable to them. So I was opposed to Air Canada setting up subsidiary companies unless they were directly related to the running of the airline, and I am still opposed to it. It seems to me that if Air Canada is to be successful, if it is to operate for the people in general rather than for a small group of businessmen, it should concentrate wholly on running the airline.
Part of the problem stems from the businessmen. Air Canada rates have gone up tremendously. Why are members of parliament not complaining about Air Canada rates? The reason is that the government pays for the tickets. The government also pays for every businessman who travels on the airline by means of tax exemptions, so that nobody really cares about the cost of the tariff on the scheduled airlines. I am sure I do not know whether the tariff is reasonable or justifiable, but we pay for the airports and for all the facilities at the airports, for weather reports and radio control as well as all the services that are provided. All the airline does is rent space. So we should be looking at the fees for scheduled airlines and whether or not the public is getting good service for their money. It is my opinion that in many areas of this country the public is not being well served by Air Canada simply because the airline is not supplying the kind of aircraft that is needed to meet the needs of the people.
It was interesting to talk to people in western Canada on this subject. There are many westerners here today who can probably comment on the services of Air Canada. The ones I spoke to told me they could not fly on scheduled Air Canada flights between Edmonton and Calgary for two reasons-and this is something that Air Canada should consider. One reason was that the aircraft landed way out of town and it was difficult to get into town from the airport at which they were landing. Second, the airline was operating on a schedule that did not satisfy the business community or the travelling public. The last time I was in that area we travelled on what they call an airbus. You buy your ticket and stand in line for a flight that leaves every hour on the hour and comes back on the half
[Mr. Peters.)
hour. It takes off at the municipal airport right in the city, and there is not much waiting at either end.
Mention has been made of the Mirabel airport. There is an easy solution to the problem at Mirabel and one that we should consider very shortly. The advertisements you see in the newspapers from Boston are only the beginning. There are few airlines that will agree much longer to go through the hastle with their customers that they have to go through now in Mirabel where passengers have to transfer to the domestic routes at Dorval. Very few airlines will put up with that for very long. They will schedule all their flights into Montreal or into Boston where services can be provided. We made a mistake with Mirabel. This government has made lots of mistakes. I do not know whether our mistake was in building Mirabel or in keeping Dorval, but it is my honest opinion that we should either close down Dorval or close down Mirabel and operate only one airport from which passengers can travel either overseas or within the country. I do not care which airport is closed down.
It would seem to me to be more sensible to close down Dorval because we have built this monster at Mirabel and no one likes facing the fact that we made such a bad mistake that we must close down the new airport. Nevertheless, we should make a decision. There are many passengers now travelling through both Mirabel and Dorval, whereas a couple of years ago they were only travelling through Dorval. Dorval can handle the passenger traffic and, I dare say, so can Mirabel, but I suggest that one of the things that we better do very shortly is close down one of those airports and arrange for the traffic to come into the gateway of Canada, whether it be at Mirabel or Dorval so that people can transfer to domestic flights at the same airport. This would make things much simpler for people travelling with a lot of luggage. It is surprising that everyone coming from overseas has more luggage than they need, a lot more luggage than they have on domestic flights. This creates a problem if you have to travel 29 miles to reach another airport and go through the same hastle at the second airport as you did at the first one.
So I suggest that if we are really serious about helping Air Canada to continue to grow, a good way to do it is to establish a board of directors rather than having the governor in council make the decisions. The board of directors should answer directly to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). He might as well run the airline. This might facilitate some things for him. Perhaps arrangements could be made which he could not make otherwise. The board of directors should be able to make decisions for Air Canada and the minister should be aware of the troubles at Mirabel and of the ways to solve them. Secondly, Air Canada should look for a 25 to 35 passenger aircraft to replace the old Viscount. I suggest that we should not take the Viscount out of mothballs. Even the Canadian government is not rich enough to afford the gasoline that plane guzzles. That was never an efficient aircraft at any time and to get it out of mothballs would be a regressive rather than a progressive step. There are small jets today that are available at a much smaller price than a DC-9. They can handle 25 to
May 31. 1977

35 passengers. They can provide service on those runs where aircraft of this type can normally be efficient and meet the needs of the community.
I think that much of Air Canada service has to be related to passengers coming off domestic flights to the trans Canada corridor or going to the international corridor, and certainly with the expenditure we have made on accounting and computerization in Air Canada, this could be utilized by all those making connection with the service from the feeder lines. Much of that could be done by Air Canada itself. I hope that before long the Minister of Transport will give us some indication of what he will do about the Mirabel problem. 1 hope he will give some indication of what he is going to do about the problems of the regional carriers. They are providing competition in a field that I think Air Canada should be involved in, that is, package tours. Schedules in regional areas could be more efficient if they could be interrelated the way train schedules used to be. When you came to a junction you could transfer to another line within a reasonable period of time. But the airlines have not so far made any such arrangements.
I think the changes being made in accounting are worthwhile. I agree with those members who said the minister should not be afraid to ask for the assistance of members of parliament for a reference of the Air Canada annual report to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. Members would have an opportunity to make their contribution to problems in their area which do not appear to be understood by the officials of Air Canada.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976   MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate my colleagues who have taken part in the debate and to commend them for some of their constructive suggestions. Air Canada is one of the best airlines in the world and as I look back over its 40 years of service to Canada I am proud of it. As a Canadian, I regard Canada's airline as my airline. It is owned by all Canadians. I want to see it improve. I want to see it serve Canadians better. I want to see Air Canada become an instrument for national unity and 1 want it to become an instrument to unlock the dynamics of growth in areas of regional disparity.
To achieve this purpose it becomes extremely important that the board of directors of Air Canada should have as its members persons drawn from every region of Canada. The lines of communication between government and the board of directors should be strong enough to ensure that government policies will be clearly interpreted and reflected in Air Canada's policies. At the same time, the operation of the airline should be the responsibility of the professional staff who are accountable for their performance to the board of directors.
It is important that government be plugged into the operation of our national airline to ensure that the national purpose is served and that the privileges it enjoys are properly exercised and also to prevent unfair competition by a national Crown company with regional air carriers. To achieve this purpose it
Air Canada
is not necessary and most certainly not desirable that the government should be involved in the day-to-day operations of the company. It should not inflict on the company its judgment in matters where it has less expertise.
The requirement that bylaws of the corporation must first be approved by Cabinet before they have any force has the favourable effect of giving the government an insight into the operation of the corporation and enables it to control changes contemplated by the board of directors. On the other hand, it also undermines confidence in the board of directors and inflicts on government the role of being a corporate babysitter with a mass of paperwork to do. The ponderous and foot-dragging result is that the corporate structure of Air Canada would be weakened and government would be the villain for holding Air Canada back from making decisions in time to compete effectively in the market place. I suggest that a more efficient process would be for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to have a personal representative on the board of directors-the government after all will soon appoint all directors-and this personal representative could keep the minister and the Cabinet informed of all activities of the board, including bylaw changes. It may also be possible and desirable that the minister be made an ex officio member of the board of directors.
The expanded role of Air Canada in a wider range of activities and the opening of new avenues for finance causes me to have mixed feelings. The entry into the hotel business, if it is profitable, can stimulate the air carrier segment of its business and hopefully reduce fares. On the other hand, losses in this field could have the opposite effect. If Air Canada is to compete effectively it needs a broader base of operations and the additional powers proposed in this bill. The use to which these powers are put and the degree to which the airline moves in the national interest of Canada will be the test of the quality of leadership of the people whom the government puts in charge of the airline and therefore of the government itself.
It is in my view extremely important that Mr. Justice Estey's recommendations delivered following the Air Canada inquiry of October 1975 be followed in one respect. I should like to quote the paragraph to which I refer:
The Air Canada Act should provide a channel for the government or the responsible minister to issue to the board of directors of the corporation policy directives where the national interest from time to time requires. Where the national interest requires the corporation to undertake routes and projects where it will be demonstrably impossible to operate at a profit in the commercial sense, the airline should undertake them for the account of the government and be reimbursed accordingly.
The reason I am so concerned about this section is that I am not convinced that transportation is now being used as a development tool in areas where other government departments and policies are attempting to focus on the root causes of regional disparity.
In the new summer Air Canada flight schedule, the city of Fredericton, which serves central New Brunswick, will lose a morning flight from Montreal and a return flight to Montreal at noon hour each day. This will result in the reduction of air seat capability and an equally severe reduction in air cargo transportation. Air Canada must feel this reduction is neces-

May 31, 1977
Air Canada
sary to cure its economic problems but it may well create them for people in New Brunswick.
The hard-nosed decision to retrench air service to central New Brunswick is a serious rejection by the federal government of the use of transportation as a development tool. It makes a mockery of the government's commitment to a policy of regional development. Indeed, this cutback was undertaken without the prior knowledge of or notice being given to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard). The war on economic disparity cannot be won in Canada by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion itself. Neither can it be won by our national airline. It requires the concentration, the combined efforts and the focus of all departments and Crown agencies, on the problem. It is not enough to have DREE spend millions of dollars on worthwhile projects in New Brunswick and other areas of Canada if the effect is to be eroded by the failure of the government to focus its fiscal, monetary, tariff and transportation policies on the same goal.
Fredericton will hold a large number of conventions this year, including over 5,000 people to the Learned Societies' conference for which Air Canada plans to put on extra flights. My initial calculation indicated that some 48 extra flights would be required; my last inquiry indicated that at least 20 were already sold out and ticketed. Extra flights were required for the graduation at the University of New Brunswick. These are only two of literally dozens of conventions and conferences that will take place during the tourist season in New Brunswick. Because the provincial and municipal governments in New Brunswick are working with the federal government to creater a climate attractive to Canadians who wish to invest in tourism-one of the principal businesses in New Brunswick- we can see evidence of new developments.
New Brunswick is trying to move ahead. For example, a Howard Johnson's motel is just about ready to open its doors in Fredericton and what happens? Because the government does not have the structure or the desire or the knowledge, our national airline celebrates the opening of the tourist season in New Brunswick with a serious cutback in facilities. It is not the fault of the airline. I realize full well Air Canada cannot be expected to fly empty planes around the sky and I do not want them to do that, but I feel the government should enable Air Canada to balance what appears to be an outstanding tourist year against an investment in our tourist industry and the development of our region.
I would like to see the accent put on more passengers at lower fares for the same or better dollar volume. We are already losing some passenger and cargo service to Delta Airlines in Maine. We have on occasion filled the flight being cancelled. On April 20 for example, it was over-sold and had to leave some passengers on the ground. Air charter seats allotted to our area were booked before the advertisements ran out. I had hoped the profits Air Canada makes from the extra flights put on to serve the Learned Societies' conference and other conventions and conferences would enable Air Canada to maintain its existing direct air ties between Montreal and Fredericton at least for the tourist season.
Excluding Eastern Provincial Airways, the Air Canada retrenchment means that our national airline will have only one flight leaving Fredericton from Montreal which connects with ongoing flights west. A later flight terminates in Montreal.
We have no rail passenger service to New Brunswick's capital city and the cutback in air service is a serious blow. It may be necessary for Air Canada to break even on its profit and loss account; but I wish the government could enable it this once to invest in New Brunswickers and display its faith in our ability to attract visitors to this most beautiful part of Canada.
I feel also that in the national interest we should do everything we possibly can to enable Canadians to travel to all parts of this great country and get to know and understand one another. There is no magic formula or blueprint for national unity. There is only human decency, understanding and tolerance-these are the things that made our country and these are the things that can preserve it. We do, however, have to learn to communicate it and one of the ways we can communicate is through our national airline operating at a break even point with unprofitable lines clearly designated and subsidized by our government.
I like the amendments to the act which will enable the government to provide compensation for unprofitable routes in the national interest. I should like also to see the department of Regional Economic Expansion and our provincial governments directly involved in the selection of the routes to be compensated. I feel that this can be accomplished without undue interference or involvement in the day-to-day operations of the company.
One final matter: I should like to see the Auditor General much more involved with the Air Canada audit. Perhaps an external audit under the general direction of the Auditor General should be considered, but I am not clear whether the Auditor General has the power to act as a joint auditor. I think it would be a good idea if the Auditor General could direct external auditors to pay particular attention to some point or, at his option, personally intercede to direct the external auditors; or with his own staff, he might expand the audit into any area he considers necessary. This point perhaps can be taken up in committee.
In conclusion, I pay tribute to all that has been achieved over the past 40 years by Air Canada and hope, when the new act is proclaimed in its final form, that it will enable Canada's airline to fly the skies safely, and make a great and effective contribution to national unity and to resolving the problems of areas of regional disparity. I certainly hope the contribution parliament makes to our national airline will enable it to have as much faith in us as we have in it.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976   MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to participate in this debate. I will not delay unduly second reading of this bill. Actually, I think I am the

May 31, 1977

last speaker on this bill on this side of the House. The debate on this measure has been excellent and hon. members have exposed many points which they think merit consideration, and have voiced their concerns. Though we all consider this bill important, we should note that the government first introduced the bill on October 28, seven months ago. Surely it could have given it higher legislative priority, particularly since we do not often have the opportunity to examine the workings of this large and important Crown corporation which affects many Canadians one way or another. It is unfortunate as well that the minister saw fit to bring forward this bill at the very time when the transport committee is travelling in eastern Canada, examining various transportation problems in the Atlantic provinces. I suggest the minister has shown contempt for the work of the committee, many members of which would like to participate in this debate. Owing to the demands of travel to Atlantic Canada, they are unable to participate.
I am greatly concerned because there is no provision for regular review of Air Canada's activities. I think a committee of the House last considered an annual report of the corporation back in 1973. Since Air Canada is a large corporation, operating with an investment of approximately $1 billion of taxpayer money, and since it is our national air carrier and carries many Canadians, surely it behooves the government to order the company to appear regularly before a parliamentary committee and thus be accountable regularly to its shareholders, the people of this country. I hope, when this bill is in committee, we shall be able to enshrine either in the legislation or in some regulation a requirement for Air Canada to appear every year before the appropriate parliamentary committee. At least, it ought to appear when so ordered by that committee. Such provision would serve not only the interests of members of parliament and the House, but would be beneficial to Air Canada. I would improve the efficiency of Air Canada's operations and of its management.
Air Canada is often criticized for its service, and I suggest many complaints and criticism are justifiable. However, I suggest if Air Canada's management were to appear before a committee regularly, it could set the record straight and answer charges and criticisms levelled against the corporation from time to time which are not justifiable. Many hon. members in the last few days have criticized Air Canada for its inadequacies and shortcomings. 1 point out that we criticize the airline with the hope of improving its operations. Our criticism was not meant to be destructive. In that connection let me say that, though I have often criticized Air Canada in the past, I think the airline's senior management under its newly appointed chief executive officer and president, Mr. Claude Taylor, is doing a good job. Since taking over the running of the corporation, Mr. Taylor has done well. He and his associates have made decisions which have made our national airline function reasonably efficiently. The airline's employee morale has improved. Drastic steps were taken to cut costs, improve efficiency, improve the utilization rate and increase productivity. By and large, the new president and his
Air Canada
board have made determined efforts to make Air Canada profitable.
The people of Canada hold various views about Air Canada. The airlines national task is not an easy one to fulfil. Many Canadians expect much of Air Canada. Bearing this in mind 1 say that, on balance, the new management has done a good job. It listened to and dealt with criticisms. However, no airline is perfect.
Many hon. members have complained about scheduling and frequency of service, with reason, I suggest. Although we complain, we must remember that one must balance costs, the cost of utilization against the cost of energy. I know, as well, that the Commissioner for Official Languages has used Air Canada as his favourite punching bag. The president of Air Canada has been preoccupied with attempts to implement some of the recommendations made in the Official Language Commissioner's report. A recent report makes 146 recommendations. Some of them arose from a recent study of the corporation's eastern region headquarters, and some appear unrealistic. Actually, some of them will tend to hurt the morale of employees and the operations of the airline, and may go far to erode the good will built up under Mr. Taylor's leadership. I hope, perhaps while we are considering this bill or when the committee has the chance to examine the company's annual report, that we can explore the recommendations and criticisms the Commissioner of Official Languages has levelled at Air Canada.
We have heard only one side of the story. I know the people working in ticket offices and on counters have been somewhat apprehensive about recommendations the Commissioner for Official Languages has made, and are even more apprehensive in case some of them will be implemented.
As others said, this year we celebrate the fortieth anniversary of Air Canada's establishment. During the past 40 years, no fundamental amendments have been made to the Air Canada Act. It is fair to say, therefore, that this bill is long overdue. In the 40 years since the first Air Canada Act was proclaimed, the corporation and the society in which it operates have undergone phenomenal growth and change. In that sense, one of the major failings of this particular piece of legislation is that nowhere in the bill is it spelled out what the mission and the role of Air Canada is intended to be.
It has been cited time and time again by former executive officers and particularly emphasized by the former chairman of Air Canada, Mr. Yves Pratte, who had this to say in testimony before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications on June 22, 1971, and I quote:
The basic problem in so far as we at the management level are concerned is that we do not know what the mission of Air Canada is. We wish we knew. It is awfully difficult to manage any organization when one does not know what the purpose of the organization is: when you are told on the one hand that the purpose of the organization is to be as profitable as any private corporation and, on the other hand, that you are to provide service at all cost.

May 31, 1977
Air Canada
The basic problem is for the government to define the role and mission of Air Canada. If that is defined, I am satisfied that we can do the job; but it is not up to us to decide what our role is.
Other speakers have pointed this out. Surely this is an appropriate time to define the role and the mission of Air Canada. Is it to provide a service at cost or is it to show a profit? Surely this legislation should provide that direction.
If Air Canada is to be a profit oriented corporation, as recent policy statements by the government seem to imply, the provisions of this bill should clearly state that. It would have the advantage of giving potential investors more confidence in the commercial orientation of this corporation. It would clear up the somewhat unnecessary ambiguities and uncertainties which are in this bill. In this connection, I want to quote somewhat extensively from a document entitled "The Evolution of Transportation Policy in Canada". It was written by Mr. John R. Baldwin who at one time was the president of Air Canada. He is dealing with the operations of two major Crown corporations, Air Canada and CNR. He states at page 41 and I quote:
There is no clear public definition why it is important that they-
That is referring to Air Canada and CNR.
-be publicly-owned or what the government expects from each that is different from private competitors. Greater responsiveness to government policies, willingness to act as a "model" corporation, and the need for a governmental instrument are generalities that have been used but mean little unless defined more specifically in a complete context of goals. Air Canada, worried by this situation a few years ago, prepared and submitted for approval to its minister a set of objectives. The company was told they were satisfactory but I would have been happier if they had become a public document opened for parliamentary debate. This could have resulted in some concurrence on the nature and purposes of public ownership, on corporate objectives, and on public expectations. The need is made greater by the insertion in the NTA of transportation principles with their commercial orientation.
I hoped something of this sort would emerge in the new Air Canada legislation but the bill submitted for first reading is silent on this point. An opportunity remains for the matter to be brought forward in parliamentary debate. I believe the same comment on value of broad parliamentary agreement on goals and objectives exists for CNR as well. I am aware that not all management may agree, some preferring the greater flexibility of a purely internal definition of objectives.
My attitude is influenced by other aspects of the first public draft of the new Air Canada legislation. While it would (or in some cases could, since permission from government would be needed) give Air Canada badly needed broader powers and improved capital structure, about 80 per cent of the principal operative clauses reserve a discretionary authority for the Governor in Council. This is a tremendous amount of power to place in the hands of the bureaucracy. It could nullify some objectives of the bill or allow intervention in management matters to a degree that would reverse the hitherto good record of government in regard to reasonable freedom for management. The Board of Directors, whose powers and role are nowhere defined in the legislation, could find themselves with little in the way of a useful role. My fear, incidentally, primarily centres on the temptation for the bureaucracy to intervene in management even more than of the intent of the Governor in Council to misuse its authority. I cannot believe that this situation will pass unnoticed.
That summarizes some of the concerns that members on this side of the House have expressed in connection with this legislation. Coming from an authority like Mr. Baldwin, it certainly deserves some very serious consideration. I hope that during the time we consider this bill that this passage will be considered in a serious manner.
The bill provides authorization for Canada to engage in activities which are not currently permitted. This act brings the question of the role of the corporation into even greater light. The proposed act broadens the capacities and activities which the company may undertake, both within and outside Canada. Aside from operating the business of an air carrier, there are references to hotels and other accommodation, surface vehicles and facilities for the transportation and housing of persons, goods and mail, services, facilities and equipment for organizing and conducting tours, catering and providing other passenger-related services, including reservations for transportation and accommodation, and computer and teleprocessing systems and technical, advisory and consulting services.
Generally the increases in these activities are good for the company. They will give it an opportunity to provide a more complete travel package. The act does this, and it is something that Mr. Baldwin referred to in his critique of the bill. All these things have to be authorized by the governor-in-council. There are two matters of concern in that connection. First, there is the potential danger of undue political interference or influence and bureaucratic intervention. Second, there is concern that it could allow the company to extend into "for-hire" trucking services, something about which the Canadian Trucking Association has expressed justifiable concern.
The Canadian Trucking Association argues that there is no reason for Crown corporations functioning in the rail or air mode to engage in "for-hire" trucking in competitions as it were to the primary function of said corporation. "For-hire" trucking has proved to be one mode where private enterprise can provide adequate service and effective competition in practically all parts of the country. I know the minister has responded. He attempted to allay the fears of the Canadian Trucking Association in this area. However, I do not believe that his response and explanation are satisfactory. We will consider that area quite thoroughly when this bill gets into committee.
Bill C-17 brings about an authority and mechanisms for transferring the ownership of Air Canada from CN to the government directly.
I think it is fair to say that the CN connection has in the past had the effect of allowing Air Canada management to effectively circumvent parliamentary control. Air Canada has received money from CN rather than directly from parliament, as well as advances of funds; a significant amount of money has been advanced in this way without reference to parliament and without any degree of accountability. The principle of trying to separate Air Canada from the CNR is one which we in this party have advocated for some time and we are very pleased that it is contained in this legislation. The former minister of transport, now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) made reference to this back in 1969.

May 31, 1977

A large part of the bill deals with the financing of Air Canada. Authorizing more common shares is rather a nonissue at present, but it may have some bearing in the future if some or all of Air Canada is transferred to the private sector. Allowing the corporation to borrow on the private market would seem to be a step in the right direction. We note that all borrowing must first be approved by the Minister of Finance. It would seem that government control is being extended into the day to day operations of the airline, and this is something at which we must take a serious second look.
The government seems to have followed Judge Estey's recommendation only half way. He said in his report that the position of the board of directors as the ultimate authority in the corporation should be improved by enlarging the board and forming an executive committee of the board. The management set-up of Air Canada has been changed to allow for this change, but the rest of the bill, in my view, circumvents it in spirit. Clause 7 is a good example. We read that all bylaws made by the board have to be approved by order in council. This crops up again in clause 8 wherein it is said that Air Canada should provide a channel for the government to issue to the board policy directives where the national interest requires.
It would appear that, here again, the government has completely lost the spirit of the Estey report. Clause 8 gives the government sweeping powers to control Air Canada. Simply stated, the act tells Air Canada to comply with any directives which it is given. No limits are placed upon what directions are permitted. To my mind, this is inexcusable. A provision in clause 9 states that the governor in council may-it is not obliged to, but it may-pay compensation to Air Canada for operating unprofitable routes in the national interest. This, surely, should be clarified. We should be told how the losses are to be calculated and how the operation is to be carried out.
A number of clauses require clarification. In some cases we find ambiguities and contradictions in the legislation, and we hope we shall be able to refine those clauses so as to make them consistent with what should be the principal thrust of the legislation. The question of auditing has been raised by other members. This issue raises the question of political pork-barrelling. Surely, if the management of Air Canada is to manage, they should have discretion in this particular area.
In summary, the principle of the bill is, in our view, long overdue and we certainly support it. We feel that the wording has taken it past the major recommendations of Judge Estey in connection with the revamping of the corporation. This is one of the first occasions on which we have had a clear analysis of the workings of the airline. We feel the bill grants undue power to the governor in council and that it could amount to what one might refer to as a supermanagement level of the public service to oversee the normal management of Air Canada, and we have some apprehensions about that.
These features could tend to transform the corporation into an agency of government rather than a commercial enterprise. Subject to appropriate government directives and control measures and accountability procedures-and I must say that
Air Canada
the word "appropriate" must be stressed here-the direction and control of the corporation should be vested in the board and in the management, and I cannot reiterate enough the fact that the corporation should be accountable to parliament, to the House of Commons, through the relevant committee.
I do not think Air Canada should be called upon to pay for some of the sins which have been committed by other Crown corporations. We have no choice but to accept as given that Air Canada is, and should be, professionally and responsibly managed. If that is not the case, the government has the means of changing the board and the management. Nevertheless, the government should not tie the hands of the company or set up a control mechanism which would demoralize the corporation and make it unattractive to those with the skills necessary to operate it at its best level.
I believe that if the corporation is given permission to manage itself within a defined set of government policies similar to the operation of a private airline and consistent with good business practice, without undue government interference, the nickname "Err Canada" may very well disappear for good. Indeed, Canada's national airline might well become an airline of which all Canadians can be proud.
We are pleased to see that this bill will now move to committee. We shall, naturally, have some amendments to introduce at that stage. We hope we shall have an opportunity to call witnesses to obtain their views and clarification of certain points. We hope, also, that the minister will be receptive to some of our suggestions, because it is in our interests to make the bill a better piece of legislation so that the Crown corporation can go forth and become a transportation entity of which we as Canadians can be proud.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976   MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take the time of the House for a few minutes to put forward some thoughts on Air Canada. It has long been a point of thoughtful observers that if the federal government ever got around to making a start in seriously cutting down spending, a useful place to start would be Air Canada. Air Canada has become fat and lazy. It has a monopoly of 75 per cent of cross-country routes, and one would have to be a very placid traveller to call the service provided much more than an indifferent one.
It is obvious we should have competition wherever possible, and in connection with the airlines it is one area which could certainly be more meaningful. But I note that the head of Air Canada has always decried the American practice of having a number of airlines competing with one another. I think it ill behooves the head of Air Canada to express such an opinion, since Air Canada has a monopoly of 75 per cent of the cross-Canada travel, come what may. CP Air and the five regional airlines would certainly be willing and able to play a more extensive role than that allowed them by the federal regulatory authority.

May 31, 1977
Air Canada
Although there is much competition in the field of railways, there is a place for it, too, in the matter of air travel. The routes which Air Canada finds least attractive are still served by private carriers at a profit, which just goes to show that Air Canada does not need to use the argument that it has "milk runs" which do not pay and hence cause a deficit. The government has protected Air Canada and set it apart from potential competitors. That may have been necessary at the beginning. It reports directly to parliament while other air carriers are governed strictly by the CTC. Air Canada, by and large, is given the most profitable routes while other airlines must be content with routes which the national airline does not want. Because Air Canada has been so zealously protected by the government, it has not been efficient or cost conscious and certainly compares unfavourably with U.S. airlines of comparable size.
Air Canada has really had everything its own way. If it wanted a route, the regulatory authority favoured its pet. An example of this was provided when Nordair applied in 1973 for a set service linking Thunder Bay, Sudbury, Ottawa and Montreal. It was a one-day flight. The CTC turned down the application when Air Canada undertook to provide comparable service, but the scheduling was such that it required a two-evening stay in Montreal for a one-day business trip.
The influence of Air Canada on the negotiators in the Department of Transport can certainly be noted. In recent trans-border allocations of routes Air Canada received 19 out of 20, the lone exception going to CP Air. In my own province of Manitoba, Transair would have been immeasurably helped by having at least one route allocated to them. It is significant that three U.S. airlines are flying out of Winnipeg south to Chicago, Minneapolis and Denver, with no Canadian alternative. As I understand it, the possibility of CP Air or Transair being allocated routes in other parts of Canada was under negotiation, and Air Canada has not even taken up some of the routes negotiated on their behalf. I feel that this crass cringing to the wishes of Air Canada by the Department of Transport is one reason CP Air has been failing to show a profit and is undergoing hard times. In any case, Air Canada always tends to show a loss.
For western Canadians, Air Canada has come to signify a largely eastern dominated airline, bringing with it the problem of language. One of the problems faced by Air Canada employees in the city of Montreal, which is its major base, is use of language. The Official Languages Act provides that in any public facility there should be a person available who is competent to speak one of the two official languages. As I say, use of one language or the other in maintenance work at Air Canada has now become a bone of contention. As I understand Bill 1, the Quebec legislature wishes the language of work in Quebec to be French. I have no quarrel with that, but it does create problems for a national airline like Air Canada. Should its employees be required to work only in French, and would this detract from their efficiency and the movement of Air Canada employees across the country? So far as cabin crews

are concerned, we would all agree that facility in the second language should be available at all times. But does this mean that all cabin crews must originate from Montreal, to the detriment of potential cabin crews in other parts of the country?
One of the ways to solve the problem of competition would be to revoke Air Canada's 75 per cent cross-country monopoly which it has. This could be done in stages so Air Canada could adjust to the increased competition. It may not be able to retain its 75 per cent of the traffic. This bill seems to make very doubtful the proposition that Air Canada will be any more efficient or economic than it has been in the past. As I have said, the airline is associated essentially with eastern Canada; western Canadians look on CP Air as their airline. Pacific Western Airlines is also expanding and becoming a larger regional airline. I hope that this bill will answer some of the questions concerning Air Canada, but I doubt that it will.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE THE MAXIMUM LIABILITY OF THE CORPORATION AND CREDIT GUARANTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill, Bill C-47, to amend the Export Development Act increases the maximum liabilities for export credits insurance and guarantees. Specifically, by amending section 26 of the act the maximum liability ceiling on insurance written for the corporation's account would be increased from $750 million to $2.5 billion. By amending section 28, the ceiling on insurance written for the account of the government would be increased from $750 million to $1 billion. This amendment to the Export Development Act will raise the present statutory limit for insurance and guarantees such that EDC may meet the full requirements of Canadian exporters through to the end of 1978.
All hon. members are aware that success in international trade is absolutely essential to the health of the Canadian economy. The export credits insurance program of EDC is a critical factor in facilitating exports. Mr. Speaker, some 25 per cent of our gross national product is attributable to Canada's exports to foreign countries. The more successful our exporters are, the more our manufacturers will be required to manufac-
May 31, 1977

ture more goods in order to meet their requirements, and in turn will be able to provide more employment, which is so needed at this time, for many, many Canadians.
The bill has had thorough discussion in committee covering all aspects of the operations of the Export Development Corporation. The co-operation and understanding of the importance of this measure by all members of the committee has resulted in an expeditious passage. Therefore, I would recommend that Bill C-47, to amend the Export Development Act, as reported from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs be passed by this House.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE THE MAXIMUM LIABILITY OF THE CORPORATION AND CREDIT GUARANTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as was indicated by the parliamentary secretary, this bill had three sessions with the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. The fact that it required three sessions should be a salutary lesson to a number of government agencies. In this particular case the government somehow or other waited until the last minute to schedule the bill before the House. Then it went over to committee, where committee members were met with the plea that the pipeline was more than full in so far as credit insurance was concerned.
I think it is wrong to say that any delay in the passage of the bill might inhibit the operations of the agency. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) will have something to say about that, but I would like to indicate that I do not think it is the proper way to operate the shop. It was clearly understood and foreseeable, as was indicated by the chairman and other officers of the corporation, that because of increased dollar values due to inflation, not only in Canada but abroad, the then existing ceilings on loans and credit insurance were inadequate for the purposes of the corporation. With a little foresight we would have had an avoidance of this procedure.
In Great Britain and other countries there may be a wall of paper built around the operations of parallel institutions; but in the United States, on the other hand, it is quite open to determine who obtained credit insurance, for what purpose, what country was involved and what parties were involved. The same thing applies to loans. In so far as the government of Canada is concerned, it is high time to emulate it. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) is trying to impress upon the whole operation of government a right to information. We should not have the situation where somebody in a government agency at some director level, or at the assistant deputy minister level or the deputy minister level can say, "It would not be in the government's interests if we let anyone know what goes on. That would be sacrosanct". There has to be a good deal more information put out.
We did get some information. In the end, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and his associates were as co-operative as they could be under the circumstances, but square one was so far down the line that other agencies which are going to come before parliament in the foreseeable future should take note of what the opposition is going to insist upon. We have a right to insist. Their operations are not going to be sacrificed
Export Development Act
or damaged in any way. Frankly, this bill took three days in committee merely to get that point across.
In so far as the operations are concerned, we know this agency is vital to Canadian trade. Canadian trade is in a tough spot. Many of our commodities are being priced out of the market by some darned foolishness at the productive levels, in government policies and in tax policies. They are hard-pressed to sell. Then there are great crocodile tears from some industries where employment has gone soft. All one has to say to those people doing the greatest crying is, "Look to your own actions in this regard".
One has to say, also, "How much have you been the author of the wrongs and the ills of your own industry? Let us see where the competitive costs are. It is not the government's role to subsidize in order to get into foreign market". This is a form of government subsidy. We have to practice it in the worldwide markets because other nations do it. If the operation of this corporation did not exist, and if these facilities were not available to Canadian business, I would say there would be a most appreciable decline in Canadian export trade and, naturally, in Canadian industry. Then we would see who would be doing the crying and the moaning.
I hope this bill will get third reading by five o'clock. The reports of the committee indicate to the members of the House information which is necessary. It being a short bill with a limited purpose, as far as I am concerned, having established the point about the right to information and that government should mend its ways with regard to the timing of these bills, I am quite prepared to recommend to hon. members that this bill be passed.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE THE MAXIMUM LIABILITY OF THE CORPORATION AND CREDIT GUARANTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of this House should bear in mind that when we are referring to the Export Development Corporation we refer to one of the largest Crown corporations that this government has under its control. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has indicated that we caught the government attempting to slip through the substance of what we have before us in Bill C-47 as a $1 item. I think their actions were wrong. They attempted to circumvent parliament, the committees of parliament and the House itself.
In requiring and asking for the ruling the Speaker gave that the $1 item was not proper we have at least secured the precedent of ensuring that the government in future, when they wish to raise the ceilings with respect to loan limits in EDC or the insurance ceilings in EDC, must do it in a proper way, and that is by amendment to the EDC legislation itself. Having said that and having once again agreed that we do not have any serious misgivings concerning the insurance side of EDC's activities, there is a caveat which I would like to mention later.
I would like to reiterate that we do have very serious questions concerning the financing activity which has become so much the lifeblood of EDC. We have come to the point
6126

May 31, 1977
Export Development Act
where we have to start asking very basic questions. Is it in the long-term interest of Canada that EDC give soft loan financing, for example, to Poland to allow that country to establish a pulp and paper industry on the strength of our credit? As far as pulp and paper exports are concerned, world competition is becoming more and more competitive, and yet we find-this was brought out in the committee-that EDC had little hesitation in going to the Bank of Warsaw in Poland and signing an agreement to lend Poland $108.7 million to help finance the purchase of equipment and related services for pulp and paper complexes in that country. We cannot get the EDC to identify what interest rate it put on that loan. We understand it is probably in the range of 7 per cent to perhaps 8.5 per cent, but we know that starting possibly as late as January, 1981, the bank in Warsaw will be given ten years to repay that loan.
I cite that as an example of the activities which EDC has started to finance, and I think a serious question must be raised as to whether those who are currently in charge of EDC, which is under the direct supervision of the government, are being prudent in making loans to a country such as Poland with a view to helping it establish a pulp and paper industry which will be competitive with our own pulp and paper activities.
During the second reading debate of this bill we indicated our basic support for its provisions. It really only raises the insurance liability ceilings of EDC. As I have said, we have always felt that the insurance side of EDC was the more credible aspect of the activities of EDC, and we believe the change in the insurance provisions is justified. However, I said that there is a caveat. In the committee there was the startling revelation that comparatively few companies in Canada are sharing the bulk of the benefits as far as the insurance activities of EDC are concerned. In 1976, 50 corporations secured insurance commitments from EDC, for a total liability of $278.9 million. That, incidentally, represented about 60 per cent of the total insurance liabilities underwritten by EDC in that year. It is pertinent to ask ourselves whether that is equitable. Is EDC doing all in its power to ensure that comparatively small concerns get the benefit of export credit insurance to a greater extent than is now being awarded to those companies?
I ask that because if we look over the list it is rather startling to see where the insurance was actually written. We were only given ranges. In spite of the fact that EDC is a Crown corporation, apparently we were not entitled to know the precise insurance policies which were written with, for example, MacMillan Bloedel. But it is interesting to note that in 1976-in fact, for the past five years-MacMillan Bloedel has been number one on the hit parade as far as insurance commitment is concerned. In 1976 that company alone received an underwriting of $30 million to $40 million. As we can see from the figures I initially gave, that is more than 10 per cent of the total business written by EDC on the export insurance side alone. Canadian Cellulose Limited, and ATCO (Eastern) Limited both received insurance underwritings of $20 million to $30 million apiece. Seaboard Lumber Sales

Company Limited and British Columbia Forest Products Limited received such insurance commitments in the range of $15 million to $20 million. The Steel Company of Canada Limited, and St. Anne Pulp and Paper Company Limited received commitments of $10 million to $15 million.
I could go through the list and indicate that $5 million to $10 million in liabilities was awarded to Campotex Limited; Gulf Oil (Canada); Lewis, Keefer and Penfield Limited; and Atlas Steels Limited, a division of Rio Algom Limited. It is obvious that EDC finds it comparatively easy to put out huge commitments for the benefit of such corporations, and our basic question is: Is EDC doing all in its power to ensure that comparatively small companies get a fair amount of assistance which should be going to them as opposed to relatively large corporations?
Dealing with this subject in the committee Mr. V. G. McKay, vice-president of finance, Export Development Corporation, stated the following:
Of the top 50 policyholders of which you have a list in the short-term section of the insurance division, approximately 60 per cent of the liability of the corporation is represented in those 50 names.
I have referred to some of those 50 names. Then after the companies had been identified I stated the following:
About 60 per cent of the total amount insured by EDC in 1976 went to 50 corporations. It totalled about $250 million-
It was actually some $270 million, which I referred to earlier.
-which means on the average they received about $5 million per company, or per concern. The top range, which is presumably MacMillan Bloedel Limited, got between $30 million to $40 million in total liabilities. Is that pattern, what we may assume for the four other years that we had before us, 1972 to 1975, roughly the experience of EDC, that the top 50 have been getting about 60 per cent of the total insurance and the ranges I have referred to are roughly that?
Mr. John A. MacDonald, chairman of the EDC, replied: "Yes". Mr. Chase-Casgrain, vice-president of the corporation in charge of insurance, replied: "Yes, I think that would be an accurate statement, Mr. Stevens". I think it is important that we put on the record that in truth a tremendous amount of the insurance activity of the EDC benefits a comparatively small number of companies. I find it inconsistent that not only is it going for the benefit of those companies-and I point out that many of the companies I referred to are big pulp and paper companies in Canada- but we find the contradiction of EDC, through their financing arm, through their lending activities, going to a bank in a country such as Poland and lending $100 million to help them set up a pulp and paper company in Poland, which in turn will presumably compete with such companies as MacMillan Bloedel who feel they need the type of insurance I have been referring to in order to sell their goods around the world. Surely there is some inconsistency in our making a $100 million loan to Poland to help them get into the pulp and paper industry so they can compete with the very pulp and paper companies to which we are giving insurance coverage to help them sell their goods around the world.
May 31, 1977

So far 1 have touched mainly on the insurance side of EDC activities because that, frankly, is the part that is covered by the bill before us raising the limits. But on this side of the House we have felt much less comfortable with the financing side of EDC than with the insurance side. The loan activities of EDC deserve a much closer scrutiny than they have been receiving, and we would like to put forward a few of our concerns, if we may, on this matter, that is, the lending activity of EDC, on the record.
We find the EDC is extending hundreds of millions of dollars in credit for the benefit of a select few countries and eventually we might have to write off substantial portions of these loans. Unfortunately, this will be done with little or no recourse or review. In a sense, you might say that it is typical of this government's actions. They blunder, they make mistakes, they act irresponsibly, such as in this case when they lend money, and subsequently we will find two years, five years or ten years from now, when these loans are not being repaid, that somehow the government will present a new nationalization. They will say, "We have a problem. We must accept a write-off against our current budgetary position", and they will step in, if they are still in power, and say, "Give us the credit, now, for clearing up the mess".
The reason we on this side of the House wish to draw attention to the irregularities and irresponsibilities in EDC is that we realize it will be this party as the government of Canada that will have to clear up some of the mess that will be left by these EDC type loans to which I have referred. In a sense, it is very typical of this government's attitude concerning the so-called national unity question. Surely, the government of the last nine years have created many of the problems in Canada that have led to a spirit of disunity. Their economic mismanagement has been so tragic as to trigger the unemployment and inflation that we have. It is natural that some people are now talking about a better system or even about some type of separation. But let us never forget that it is this government that in the past nine years has created the fertile ground for those feelings to spring from. Yet now we find how ludicrous it is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and even certain of his cabinet ministers, are pretending that they are the people to unify the nation and set it all right again.
In no way is the Canadian public vulnerable to such a lie. The responsibility must be pinned where it should be pinned, and that is on the government for their gross mismanagement of the economic and other affairs of this country. That is why I am so concerned about the irresponsibility that is taking place with respect to financing through EDC. Only last weekend we had the government House leader gratuitously offering a write-off of some $250 million with respect to debts owed by other countries to this country. How nice it is to casually say that we will write off that money. But let me emphasize that that type of write-off is only the beginning of what may happen with regard to some of the loans that are being made by EDC. Further write-offs will be required. Later in my remarks today I want to suggest that it is time the government
Export Development Act
started to reserve those write-offs in their budgetary figures that will occur with respect to some of the so-called soft loans that EDC is making.
We have already seen how the government tried to slip $2 billion in additional authorized EDC insurance liability through the House as a $1 item. Both my colleague and I have referred to it. We opposed this, and the bill before us is a result of the objections we had at that time to that sleight of hand. But the sleight of hand continues, I suggest, especially, as 1 have said, in the loan activities of EDC.
It is not a partisan pronouncement that I am making. The Auditor General himself has expressed concern about some of the write-offs that are developing and showing already in EDC. Let me quote from page 42 of the last report of the Auditor General, dated March 23. He stated:
The future economic and political conditions in some of the countries where the corporation has made loans are unpredictable and accordingly possible losses to the corporation are not susceptible to accurate measurement.
We find that with a little juggling and accounting gymnastics-the polite term is "rescheduling"-the government is able to carry some $61 million in defaulted loans by simply rewriting them as new or extended loans. What a convenient term! If any of us, for example, get into default with our bank, how nice it would be to merely go to the bank and suggest that they reschedule. By rescheduling, all that is meant is that you take the defaulted loan, you add accrued interest, issue a new note, and say it is now current. That is exactly the type of game that EDC has been playing with respect to over $60 million of the loans now on their books. When we questioned this practice in committee, the president of EDC, John A. MacDonald, told us that although rescheduling was necessary in some instances, the corporation in fact-
-did not make loans to a country that has been rescheduled for some considerable period of time.
What Mr. MacDonald was referring to was the simple fact that perhaps he was a little embarrassed. It was so obvious that they were carrying loans that had been rescheduled. He hastened to assure us that if a country has got into that plight, the rescheduled loans are needed and they do not make fresh loans to that country. When we checked, as we did in committee, we found that this considerable period of time referred to by Mr. MacDonald is in many cases much shorter than one would expect. Pakistan, for example, had rescheduled loans totalling $26.3 million in 1976, yet we find that early in this year, on January 27, the EDC advanced another $1.4 million to support export sales to that country.
There are also other examples, such as the case of the Philippines which has also apparently worked its way back into EDC's good graces. In the Philippines we have financed another $1.7 million, even though that country has had to reschedule $7.4 million of previous loans. It is not that we oppose this type of generosity to struggling nations but, rather, that we are concerned about the mounting payments that will have to be made by both the nations that I have referred to, other nations and Canada, as debt is piled upon debt.
80016-47%

May 31, 1977
Export Development Act
It is time we examined our goals in this area and re-evaluated our policies. As the cycle of default mounts in the world, the ability of the Export Development Corporation to promote export trade is less feasible. At home we have a federal government that in the current year is running up a deficit of $7.2 billion-a record deficit of staggering proportions in light of last year's deficit of only $5 billion. This is the same federal government that has allowed our trade to deteriorate to a deficit position, as far as manufactured end products are concerned, of some $10 billion. This is the same government that has been so oblivious to date about our current account deficit of $4.3 billion and which now appears to blithely turn its back on mounting default being incurred with respect to loans previously made to certain countries.
Let me put it this way, Mr. Speaker. Domestically we have a government that has incurred a deficit this year of $7.1 billion; externally we have a government that is living with deficits of between $4 billion and $5 billion on current account and which, in effect, is encouraging corporations and provinces to borrow sufficiently from foreign sources to cover that kind of deficit. Most important in relation to Bill C-47, we also have the EDC directing loans to support export sales, but the loans themselves will not be repaid in their entirety in future years. That is the picture we have before us-three levels of debt being piled on debt.
If I remember correctly, at committee it was revealed that somewhere in the neighbourhood of 40 per cent of all manufacturing trade from Canada not going to the United States was underwritten by the EDC at the present time. Some place along the line we have to see the significance of this measure. Granted, we want work for Canadians today, and if financing is needed we can understand the desire of the government to help. But let us not delude ourselves. We must realize that in order to generate $1 million worth of work, the EDC is lending $1 million to some country for up to 15 years and that probably a substantial portion of that amount will never be repaid.
The more this indirect subsidization snowballs, the higher the probability of default and the more we have loaded debt upon debt. For the sake of an export sale today we are literally jeopardizing jobs for future Canadians. The government should begin now to set up meaningful reserves against this type of loan so that it will not be so hard to digest in future years.
In looking over the activities of the EDC we must also question the wisdom of soft loans to communist bloc nations. We have seen EDC advance financing to Yugoslavia, Poland, Cuba, Czechoslovakia, Rumania, Hungary and Bulgaria. In one case the EDC advanced $250 million. A loan was advanced to a pulp and paper operation in Poland, yet the president of EDC admitted that it is likely this operation would be a significant competitor with our own pulp and paper industry. He justified the loan on the basis that if we did not lend the funds, somebody else would and in effect we would end up with no loaf as opposed to half a loaf. I suggest it is

shortsighted to subject this nation to the debt load the government has assumed. It is not in the best interests of Canada to continue such shaky loan activity to support international trade.
At committee we asked the minister to give us some evidence of the government's restraint in the international arena to insure that so-called soft loans will not balloon even more within a few years. I am pleased to say he indicated their concern with the type of relatively poorly secured long-term financing that is taking place. I hope we can work in conjunction with the other countries that have been active in this type of soft loan system to tighten the rules in order to ensure that Canada and the other nations in future are selling goods, not financing, as far as the export trade is concerned.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, in principle we have nothing against extending the insurance activity of EDC as contemplated in Bill C-47. We believe that is the more respectable side of EDC activities, but we feel that it should make a more sincere effort to have that insurance available to many more small businesses in the country than is the case at the present time. To have 60 per cent of the benefit of the insurance going to 50 of the largest corporations in the country is questionable. We are concerned about EDC lending activities because we think we are going to regret the day we made many of the loans that it is now publicizing with great glee in the name of supporting Canadian jobs. They may temporarily give work to Canadians, but in the long run there are going to be severe losses not only in the economic sense but in the sense of job creation in future years.
