speakeroldname: Mr. Eldon M. Woolliams (Calgary North) moved
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO RAISE AGE OF CONVICTION OF YOUNG OFFENDERS
speechtext:
that Bill C-225, to amend the Criminal Code (young offenders), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, time being limited in private members' hour I shall not, as I usually do, speak without notes but will refer to my notes closely. I hope the government will listen with sympathy to the subject I am about to discuss. I take great pleasure in speaking to Bill C-225, my own bill, which seeks to amend a Criminal Code provision concerning young offenders. In order that hon. members may understand the purpose of this bill, I shall read two sections of the Criminal Code of Canada. Section 12 reads:
No person shall be convicted of an offence in respect of an act or omission on his part while he was under the age of seven years.
That means, in brief, that any person seven years of age can be convicted of a criminal offence, with one exception to which I shall allude in a moment. In short, the Criminal Code treats any person over the age of seven as if he is an adult. The exception is contained in section 13, which reads:
No person shall be convicted of an offence in respect of an act or omission on his part while he was seven years of age or more, but under the age of fourteen years, unless he was competent to know the nature and consequences of his conduct and to appreciate that it was wrong.
In other words, any person between the ages of 7 and 14 can be convicted of a criminal offence, provided he was competent to know the nature and consequences of his conduct and to appreciate that it was wrong. Lawyers in the House will know that that rule is almost identical with the M'Naghten rule concerning insanity. In brief, my amendment would raise the age in section 12 to 12 years. It would raise the age limit from 7 years to 12 years. In other words, no person shall be convicted of an offence in respect of an act or omission on his part while he is under the age of 12 years. Surely that is a reasonable request. Surely that outdated part of the Criminal Code which is nearly 100 years old should be thrown out.
My bill would provide, second, that no person shall be convicted of an offence under the code while he is 12 years of
Criminal Code
age or more but under the age of 16, unless he is competent to know the consequences of his conduct. In brief, at present under the Criminal Code a child of eight years can be convicted of murder, manslaughter or robbery with violence, if he knew what he was doing, knew the nature and consequence of his conduct and knew it was wrong. That is the present law of Canada. I will put on record today some shocking statistics concerning the treatment of children in Canada who have been convicted of offences under the code. I shall speak of children under the age of 14 and as young as 12 years. Such children have been sent to penitentiary, there to be incarcerated with adults.
The last time I moved this bill in the House was March 3, 1970, seven long years ago. At that time children were being incarcerated in our penitentiaries. They had been incarcerated in penitentiaries as early as 1964, six years before I introduced the bill the first time. I want to deal with a case of a 12-year old boy who was sentenced by a judge in this country. I want to quote what Mr. Allan MacLeod, the superintendent of penitentiaries in Canada, said to Mr. Bill Trent, at that time a Weekend staff writer. At that time I was happy to have in my office Mrs. Robbin Frazer, who helped me do some research into this question. I now read what Mr. Bill Trent wrote:
Henri had all the cards stacked against him. He was the product of a shiftless father and a prostitute mother, who had separated. In his short lifetime he had been in all sorts of trouble. He had been sentenced to reformatories and at one time had even been committed to a mental hospital.
Then one night, during a period of freedom, he walked into the house to find his mother sleeping with her landlord. Furious, he picked up a can of tomatoes and hurled it at the man, striking him in the head. He was charged with assault.
The judge considered the matter for some time. The nature of the boy's previous offences indicated that he was in serious need of help. But there were no facilities for handling such a case.
At present the law says any person seven years old or older can be charged as an adult. I continue:
The judge Finally sentenced Henri to two years in St. Vincent de Paul, admitting he was worried about the sentence-worried whether the inmates would be a bad influence on the boy, or whether the boy would be a bad influence on the inmates.
I question the latter point. I continue:
Henri was escorted behind the high walls of the maximum-security institution-
I have been to that institution as a visitor. I continue:
-a 12-year old boy among hundreds of hardened criminals.
"I still choke up when I think about it," says Lionel St. Pierre, warden of St. Vincent's federal training centre, who was penitentiary psychologist when the boy arrived. "I hustled him into my office to keep him away from the inmates and arranged to have him transferred to Federal Training Centre."
Henri (who was later released and has apparently been keeping out of trouble) was a polite, wholly co-operative child who responded well to the sympathetic guards.
The guards liked him so well that they chipped into a fund to buy him a scooter, a toy construction set and a fleet of toy trucks.
"It was quite a sight," one of the guards told me, "to see the boy pushing his way around the prison yard on his scooter."
But St. Pierre thinks the saddest incident of all was the day he took Henri into his office.
"The boy had one request and I couldn't grant it," he recalls. "He asked me if it would be all right to go out and play in the streets until supper time."

May 31, 1977
Criminal Code
One hopes Henri's case will not be duplicated. As a result of the crusade I conducted personally in 1963 and 1970, children were removed from federal penitentiaries where they were raped, forced into homosexual acts, and learned the tricks of hardened criminals. Since 1968 the Trudeau government has promised to introduce a young offenders act. We are about as close to getting that bill as we are to having unity in this country. Both promises have been broken and both situations are in the same disarray.
With the files and research I have done-the files are more than one foot deep in my office-and since I am a trial lawyer and have for a number of years conducted cases regarding the custody of children and children getting into difficulty, 1 find that 90 per cent of such cases are the result, I am sorry to say, of irresponsibility of adults, of broken homes and the conduct of parents which in some cases is only fit for publication in Penthouse and Playboy. An article written by Pierre Berton puts the point pretty well. He wrote in part:
One byproduct was homosexuality. Since young offenders were often dumped into prison compounds with old and hardened men, it was almost axiomatic that any youth entering prison (and there were children as young as 13 in Canadian penitentiaries in the 1960's) be forced into homosexual alliance that could scar him for life.
Since 1908 there have been no real changes in the Juvenile Delinquents Act. The Diefenbaker government set up a committee in 1962 to study the whole question of young offenders. The head of that committee was Allan J. MacLeod, and the others where Dr. L. P. Gendreau, Inspector E. W. Willes, Ronald R. Price, and Miss M. L. Lynch. I might say, for the benefit of the Hansard reporter, that I am reading from my notes and he will find all these names mentioned in the text. I say this since I know I am speaking rapidly. That committee recommended, or said that the term "juvenile delinquent" was a belittling one which does not recognize the dignity of youth. They said it should be changed to "young offenders", but the federal government has done nothing despite the framework of a new act which was recently circulated by the Solicitor General's department. After my speech of March 7, 1974, and as a result of the crusade which had been under way long before that date, I managed to get most of the children out of jail by bringing pressure to bear on appropriate authorities and getting the support of the media.
I am still sad to say that today recent statistics are most revolting and disconcerting. Mr. Speaker, at present five inmates 16 years of age are incarcerated in federal penitentiaries. In addition, there are 38 inmates 17 years old and 1,343 inmates between the ages of 18 and 21. Those are national figures applying to 1973. The figures for all Canada with regard to juveniles only are as follows: There are 863 males incarcerated and 557 females, for a total of 1,520 such juveniles. I have not been able to get the 1976-77 figures for all across Canada. However, I was able to obtain figures from Canada's largest province, Ontario, and I stress that the federal government itself has left the vacuum.
The provinces have had to set up training schools at their own expense and children now have been transferred to these schools from penitentiaries; or, on the other hand, they have
[Mr. Woolliams.)
been there confined in their later years instead of being confined with adults in federal penitentiaries. The figures for Ontario for 1975 are as follows: 25 children aged 12 in training schools, 71 aged 13, 204 aged 14, 384 aged 15, and 34 aged 16, for a total of 718. To make matters worse, in 1975 for the age group of young people up to 16 there was a 50 per cent rate of recidivism, meaning that they returned to the same or another institution as the result of crimes committed.
[DOT] (nio)
I was shocked when I read the magazine "Like It Is- Young and In Trouble", publisher Gary C. Price. I checked it out today. It contains stories of what is going on in the training schools across this country. Let me take a few moments to tell the story of Tony. I will not give his last name as that would be unfair to him. Tony, now aged 23, is serving a three-year term in Collin's Bay penitentiary for armed robbery. History: his father died when he was two years of age. He was mistreated by his stepfather, never given a chance, was caught stealing at a very young age, sentenced to St. Joseph's training school at age 13 for truancy.
Fancy sending a person to a training school, a prison, for truancy! At that time he weighed 75 pounds. He was repeatedly beaten by the staff and fellow inmates. He ran away and was caught by the RCMP and handcuffed, but the handcuffs were so large that they kept falling off his wrists. He was returned to school, his head shaved and placed in a padded cell for a six-week period. He started a life of crime.
What about little Peter? Peter's parents broke up. He was sent to live with an 89-year old grandmother. Children's Aid took him away and placed him in a detention home, for truancy. At age 11 he was sentenced to a training school for breaking into a parking meter. He was taken to Cobourg training school in handcuffs. He was beaten by his instructor with his fists and maintains that a nine-year old companion was beaten and kicked because he wet his bed. Finally, he was sent to a reformatory and later a penitentiary.
At age nine Michael was caught stealing. At age ten he was caught again and sent to a training school. A militaristic atmosphere prevailed at the training school. He was attacked by inmates and sometimes forced to bend over for hours with his head in a locker. In this case it is alleged that he was forced to stand against a wall on tip toes with his forefingers pressed against the wall. Thumbtacks were placed under his heels so he could not step back. Punishment was finished when the child had to step back on the tacks.
I can go on quoting experiences for a long time, but there it is. I am of the opinion that Judge Thompson of Ontario, in the Ministry of Community and Social Services at Queen's Park, has the answer. For example, if a person of ten commits murder, or putting it softer, kills someone, he should not be labelled an offender and should be placed under child welfare care. If he has a good home, well and good, he can get the necessary guidance from home. If the home is a seriously depraved one, he should be placed where he can get help from psychiatrists and psychologists and, above all, receive some
May 31, 1977

degree of affection in line with what the average child receives in a normal home. That is all that children want, the same love and affection that the average child gets in a normal home.
1 recommend that hon. members read the John Howard Society of Ontario's response to proposals for new legislation to replace the Juvenile Delinquents Act. There they point out the same kind of treatment that Dr. Thompson set out. I plead with the minister and with the House to remove the windowdressing from reform and get on with the job. Stop image building. Images will be built if you perform. It will take a lot of public relations firms to cover up for the sins of this generation when history is written. When the image builders are dead, the historians will bone-pick the raw, cold carcass of this civilization and the truth will be revealed.
We naturally get enraged and become emotionally disturbed when we see children in the training schools. I have been in training schools in my province. My partner defended someone under the age of 13 on a murder rap. I went to see him last summer because my partner was on holiday. I know how he was confined. If there are to be places of incarceration in reference to their offences and convictions, maybe the wrong people are being put in jail. Maybe it should be somebody else who is responsible for their birth, or it might even be us, the legislators. It is time we moved on, Mr. Speaker. Charles Dickens wrote, "The Law is an ass." Well, this law is an ass. Let us ride that donkey out of the parliamentary pasture. I thank hon. members for listening to me.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO RAISE AGE OF CONVICTION OF YOUNG OFFENDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I first want to congratulate the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) for his inspiring speech and graphic illustrations pertaining to children who have suffered in penitentiaries because of their acts. He is to be congratulated for bringing forth Bill C-225 to amend the Criminal Code (young offenders). It is very timely and should be considered by all Canadians. I note the explanatory notes which state:
Under the present state of the law, no person under the age of seven years shall be convicted of an offence, this constituting a presumption de jure, and no person between the age of 7 and 14 can be convicted unless he was competent to know the nature and consequence of his conduct, this constituting a presumption juris tantum, that is rebuttable.
The purpose of this bill is to provide that no person under the age of 12 years shall be convicted and to raise also from 7 to 12 and 14 to 16 the interval during which the presumption juris tantum is applicable.
The bill provides also that no person under the age of 16 may be sentenced to imprisonment in a penitentiary as it is now possible for a delinquent, under the present state of law, in some cases.
This was pointed out graphically in the illustrations of the hon. member for Calgary North. We are concerned with sections 12 and 13 of the present act which read as follows:
12.	No person shall be convicted of an offence in respect of an act or omission on his part while he was under the age of seven years.
13.	No person shall be convicted of an offence in respect of an act of omission on his part while he was seven years of age or more, but under the age of 14 years unless he was competent to know the nature and consequences of his conduct and to appreciate that it was wrong.
It is an anachronism that the Criminal Code now contemplates that a child as young as seven can attract criminal responsibility. Therefore, in rising to speak on Bill C-225 I
Criminal Code
might say that I have a great deal of sympathy for part of the philosophy that, as I understand it, lies at the root of this bill. I suggest that this House is probably generally in accord with the thesis that children under the age of 12 should not be considered criminally responsible. I understand that in practice a relatively small percentage of juvenile delinquents adjudged to have committed a delinquency under the Juvenile Delinquents Act are under 12 years, and that most children under 12 are dealt with under the appropriate provincial child welfare or youth protection legislation.
The report of the Department of Justice Committee on Juvenile Delinquency in 1965 recommended that the minimum age of criminal responsibility be set at 10 or, at most, 12. Bill C-192, the young offenders bill, contained a provision to raise the minimum age to 10. The recent report of the Solicitor General's Committee on Young Persons in Conflict with the Law recommended raising the minimum age to 14. I understand that the responses received during the consultations held across Canada suggest support for the proposal of the hon. member for Calgary North to raise the minimum age to 12. In the report "Young Persons in Conflict with the Law" it is recommended that the minimum age under any new youth delinquency legislation should be 14. I quote from the report:
This would not imply that anyone under the age of 14 could perform harmful acts with impunity. Rather, the committee proposes that children below the age of 14 should not come under the jurisdiction of criminal legislation, but would be more appropriately looked after under the provisions of provincial child welfare, youth protection and juvenile correction legislation.
In May, 1976, the Canadian Council of Juvenile and Family Court Judges drafted a working paper on the report, the judges contending that the minimum age should be 12. They concluded:
-that 12 and 13-year olds are committing offences of sufficient seriousness that child welfare authorities will be unable or unwilling to assume responsibility for them.
There is certainly evidence to support this contention. In 1973, Statistics Canada reported that of 553 juvenile delinquents aged 12, 17 were convicted of common assault, one of assault causing bodily harm, 181 of crimes against property with violence and 6 of carrying offensive weapons. Of 1,137 juveniles aged 13, 27 were guilty of common assault, of assault causing bodily harm and danger with intent, 357 of crimes against property, with violence, and 11 cases of carrying offensive weapons. I believe these figures illustrate the fact that 12 and 13-year olds are capable of committing a wide variety of offences that cannot be shrugged off or taken lightly. Assault with intent to cause bodily harm is no laughing matter.
The remaining two provisions, however, present difficulties which I suggest will require further consideration. The second provision in the bill is to extend the application of what is known as the doli incapax rule so that persons aged 12 but under 16 should not be convicted unless shown to be competent to know the nature of their conduct and appreciate that it was wrong. The doli incapax rule under section 13 of the Criminal

May 31, 1977
Criminal Code
Code pertains now to persons of 7 years but under the age of 14. This rule is based on a rebuttable presumption that a child between the ages of 7 and 14 is incapable of committing a crime. Blacks Law Dictionary, fourth edition, defines doli incapax as the following:
Incapable of criminal intention or malice; not of the age of discretion; not possessed of sufficient discretion and intelligence to distinguish between right and wrong to the extent of being criminally responsible for his actions.
Thus, in order to establish criminal liability the prosecutor is required to show that the child has the competence to know the nature and consequences of his crime and to appreciate that it was wrong. The Department of Justice Committee on Juvenile Delinquency recommended the abolition of the doli incapax rule. The report noted that juvenile court judges were not then familiar with the doli incapax rule and that in any case the rule is difficult to apply. I would like to quote from the report which explains the reasoning for the abolition of the doli incapax rule:
The rule was formulated at a time when there were no juvenile courts and when the penalties of the criminal law were extremely harsh. Having regard to the difficulty in interpreting and applying the rule, and to the modest sanctions available under the present law, we doubt that there is any real advantage in retaining the rule. It is important to note also that the presumption weakens with the advance of the child's years towards fourteen. Its principal value is in connection with proceedings against offenders who are very young. Our proposal for raising the minimum age of criminal responsibility would further diminish the need for the rule. Finally, we think that the basic objective that the doli incapax rule is designed to serve can be accomplished more effectively through flexible disposition provisions.
That quotation can be found on page 54 of the report of the Department of Justice Committee on Juvenile Delinquency. The committee's report on Young Persons in Conflict with the Law also recommended that the doli incapax rule be abolished. Its recommendation was based on the rationale that in setting out the age jurisdiction of the proposed legislation to replace the Juvenile Delinquents Act, young persons between 14 years and under 18 should be held responsible for their illegal acts. Such an age range, however, would not prevent any province, on the basis of administrative policy, to choose not to apply the federal legislation if the circumstances of a given case demonstrated that a young person would be more appropriately dealt with under provincial legislation or that he should not be proceeded with at all.
If we increase the minimum age of criminal responsibility to 12, I would be inclined to support the recommendations of the two committees to abolish the doli incapax rule. This is based on the premise that young persons between 12 and 16 generally have the competence to know the nature and consequences of their conduct and appreciate the wrongfulness of their acts and thus should be held responsible for any illegal acts. At the same time, I support the philosophy that young persons in this age group are still in their formative years and that, generally, sanctions for their illegal behaviour should be more limited and, I believe, more specialized than those applicable to adults. They should receive special services to meet their needs, which are distinctly different from those that are available to adults.
I would like to turn to the provision in the hon. member's bill which calls for the use of industrial schools instead of the
penitentiary system for young offenders convicted under the provisions of the Criminal Code. Under certain circumstances this may prove to be impossible. It is clear that the hon. member would like to protect a youthful offender from the hardened types he is likely to encounter in the "pen". Having been a member of the subcommittee investigating the penitentiary system in Canada, I can fully endorse that point of view. Some of the inmates I met were quite unsavoury and a young offender, it seems to me, would be at the mercy of such individuals. Instead of providing rehabilitation, the penitentiary would become a school for crime.
However, we are also faced with the problem of combining youths who have committed the crime of car theft-"joy-riding"-and a youth who has been convicted of murder. Under these circumstances the provisions the hon. member has put forward would be extremely impractical, not to mention unsafe. If a youth was convicted of murder-and in 1973, 5 youths between the ages of 14 and 17 were convicted of this crime-could we really expect him to serve his sentence of a minimum of 10 to 25 years, or for the rest of his life, in an institution designed for the custody and rehabilitation of youths who have committed, relatively speaking, of course, minor offences?
One of the proposals contained in the report of the Solicitor General's committee would partially meet the intent of the bill, and would in my opinion be more realistic. It would provide for a young person who has been transferred to adult court and sentenced to a term of imprisonment to be kept in a place of secure custody as defined under the federal juvenile legislation until age 21 after which, if his term of imprisonment is to continue, he would be transferred to a place where he might ordinarily have been imprisoned. In this regard, the proposal meets the intent of preventing the confinement of any person under the age of 16 years in a penitentiary and yet it is more realistic in allowing a young person to be transferred to an adult institution by the time he reaches the age of 21. This would likely facilitate rehabilitation as well as custodial treatment.
While I support in principle the provision to increase the minimum age of criminal responsibility and the intent of the provision to avoid the confinement of any person under the age of 16 in a penitentiary, I cannot support this bill as it now stands. I understand that the ministry of the Solicitor General has been working intensively on the development of proposals for new legislation to replace the Juvenile Delinquents Act. The Solicitor General's committee's report on Young Pesons in Conflict with the Law has been used as a basis for nationwide consultations on a broad range of issues, including those raised in this bill.
One such consultation is the working paper put out by juvenile and family court judges to which I referred earlier. I do not think it is desirable at this time to make specific changes to the Criminal Code affecting age limits. We must look at the whole problem of the young offender. We must contemplate how the age changes will bear on the philosophy,

May 31, 1977

principles, the delivery of services by the provinces, and other related matters.
We must also look into the facilities that currently exist in the provinces. Are there enough institutions now to house youthful offenders if we pass this bill? I understand that at present the province of British Columbia is rethinking its approach to the juvenile delinquent. That rethinking includes the reinstitution of training schools into the correctional process. We can hardly agree to send a youth to an industrial school that does not yet exist. We must also consider the auxiliary services that we would require as well as buildings and thoroughly qualified and trained staff. Certainly there are many individuals who would qualify, but are there enough?
1 suggest, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. colleague from Calgary North withdraw his bill for the time being. Once the Department of Justice and the Solicitor General's office have had time to assess the results of the consultative process, I believe the government will be putting forward its proposals for changes to the Juvenile Delinquents Act and the Criminal Code. At that time the hon. member can make known his views on this very important subject, for I am certain that the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) will seek the views of all those who have a material interest in the subject matter before any legislation is introduced.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few comments to make on this very important bill. 1 think great credit is due to my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) for the interest he has shown in this very important topic and for bringing forward this bill. Not only has he demonstrated his interest on this occasion, but in the past he has been responsible for placing very great emphasis on legal reform as it pertains to better treatment of youthful offenders.
I was very impressed as well with the remarks of my friend, the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson), an excellent member of parliament who has many times shown his concern for matters of law reform and the protection of civil rights and liberties. Whenever such occasion has risen the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore has been in the forefront of those who have made an active and valuable contribution.
It seems to me that the principles implicit in this bill moved by the hon. member for Calgary North should find general agreement not only with members of parliament but with all people who are concerned with law reform and the rehabilitation of young offenders. I think it is fair to say that more selective and humane treatment of young people under our criminal law is long overdue. I trust that government will continue this impetus and that before long, as the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore has said, action is taken on a wide front, not just under the Criminal Code.
It seems to me to be rather paradoxical, judging from my own limited experience, that there appears to be in some areas of the civil law greater understanding of the foibles and
Criminal Code
unpredictability of youth than there is under the criminal law. I guess all of us who have practised law are aware that, while it might be frivolous to say that every dog is entitled to his first bite, there is a certain amount of truth to this in the matter of liability which accrues to young people and their parents under the civil law.
If, for example, a young person commits an act of destruction for which ordinarily such person would be directly accountable, as indeed their parents may be accountable in extreme circumstances, but it can be demonstrated that this is the first time the act has been committed and that there is no propensity shown for this kind of act, then in most cases, as I understand the law, such a juvenile is, in effect, permitted to have his first bite, to commit that one act of destruction, with the hope that all concerned will learn a lesson.
Surely since this kind of tradition under the common law has grown up over the centuries in terms of civil liability, it is time we took a very hard look at the attitude that continues to be reflected in the Criminal Code which, as my hon. friend from Calgary North so eloquently said, results in an unbelievable perversion of justice whereby young people between seven and 12 years of age under certain circumstances are incarcerated, so long as they appreciate the nature and quality of their act, and thus suffer the type of fate detailed in some of the incidents and statistics quoted by the hon. member for Calgary North.
I suggest that the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), all concerned members of parliament, the ministers of justice and attorneys general of the provinces should take this opportunity which is afforded in the House of Commons of Canada to rethink this situation, and once more make a commitment to join together either to bring in specific measures of the type implicit in this bill or, as the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore has suggested, to move ahead in a different area and provide some social measures by way of legislation which will alleviate the situation.
Indeed, in the context of social reform, it seems to me that it would not be inappropriate, either through educational means or through other measures, to put more responsibility on the parents of children who are perfectly able to give their children better training and assume more responsibility for them. When these parents find their offspring in difficulty and it appears that the parents have wilfully neglected their responsibility as parents, then I feel some of the blame-indeed, some sanction may be necessary on the part of society-should fall upon them, as well as upon the children they have failed.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker, by congratulating both my learned friends for their remarks today. I just wanted to say a few brief words in support of the propositions which they have put forward.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill C-225 let me say at once that I have a great deal of sympathy for part of the philosophy which, as I understand it, is at the root of this particular bill. It is on this basis that I congratulate the hon.
6134

May 31, 1977
Criminal Code
member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). He is a learned trial lawyer and certainly has displayed both inside and outside the House his deep concern for judicial reform.
Youth in conflict with the law is paramount in the minds of many Canadians. Young people are involved in such serious offences today as robbery, assault, etc. From time to time I receive letters from constituents who are very concerned and frustrated because they feel there is nothing the law can do to protect them from young offenders.
Recently police in my own area were conducting investigations concerning young offenders who were involved in a protection racket. Many of the people who were victims of this racket came to see me because they were very frustrated that the law could do very little to protect them. Other incidents I have heard of involved young offenders who live in public housing units; they vandalize these units and assault the people who live in them, particularly senior citizens.
Also of equal importance, those of us who served on the sub-committee on justice and legal affairs which was examining conditions in our penitentiaries were told that the average age of offenders in the Canadian penitentiary system is 27 years. We also heard some very tragic stories concerning inmates in maximum security institutions who entered the penal system at a very early age. Many of them entered our system at the age of 12 or 13 years. They started out in foster homes, graduated to industrial training schools, then went through the provincial jail system, finally ending up in the "big house" or what we call the maximum security institution. Fortunately many of these offenders are doing some of their time now in medium and minimum security institutions, most of them being out on day parole. It is this kind of tragedy which is the reason that I and the hon. member for Calgary North, as well as the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) and the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), are very concerned about the whole issue of young offenders.
I can cite some examples. When the subcommittee was travelling in the Atlantic region, we heard the story of a young individual who was incarcerated at the age of 13 years old in a maximum security institution, for stealing a car which really, in effect, amounted to no more than joyriding. At the time we talked to that individual he was 36 years of age. Thus, for some 23 years he had been in and out of our penal system.
I am sure it almost goes without saying that there are many cliches which people talk about that are true; but when a young person goes into the "big house" or a maximum institution, he is subject to a lot of pressure, a lot of harassment, and is also subject to learning the tools of the trade. In effect he graduates to much more serious crime and becomes very involved with that particular element. When we looked at that particular individual, he was in solitary confinement, and he certainly was a security risk. I made some inquiries about him, asking why he was in solitary confinement and why he was considered to be that much of a security risk. The authorities

replied, "You look at him. You can see he is a security risk because he has taken a hostage, raised a lot of problems, caused vandalism within the institution, ransacked his cell, caused fires, broke the toilet in his cell, and also broke the sink. Also, on a number of occasions, he has worked with others and conspired with others attempting to escape. Certainly he should be classified as a security risk."
In talking to the classifications officer and to the psychologist working in the institution at that time, we found out that back in the history of this individual we could have certainly done something with him at the time of the original sentence which was for, to all intents and purposes, no more than joyriding, and yet he was charged with and convicted of stealing a motor vehicle. He was charged in the adult courts and placed in a maximum security institution. These are the kinds of tragedies we see in small numbers within our federal penal institutions. Even though they are in small numbers, it happens too often. There may be many that are not reported.
There are other instances where we see people 35-36 years of age who are serving time in our maximum institutions who literally get burned out, as they say, and tired of dealing with the entire system. They are tired of dealing with maximum security institutions, of going in and out like a revolving door and finally get to the point where they say "I have had enough". It is at that particular time they feel they should try and rehabilitate themselves, and they do so. There have been some very good success stories and testimonies from a number of these individuals. One of them we heard was from a man who is now doing work with young people, retarded people and young offenders, in the Atlantic region. At some point in time, if we had a proper set of laws to deal with such offenders, and proper programs to deal with them, it goes without saying that we could do something with them and save this very valuable resource, our youth.
It almost goes without saying, and for that matter it is almost a cliche, that the problems will not be resolved through bills like Bill C-225 or any other legislative reform dealing with young offenders. It requires community involvement and initiative. It also requires other imaginative governmental programs, like the creation of the Ministry of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport. Young people need to be active, and it is the government's responsibility and the community's responsibility to provide opportunities for youth.
In my own particular area we have a very high rate of young offenders. During some of the meetings with my community workers and people who work in my area I found, much to my surprise, that in one particular area, which has one of the highest rates of juvenile offenders-the Mount Pleasant area-the community facilities were closed at six o'clock in the evenings. That is the time the majority of our young people are looking for some facility where they can go and play basketball, badminton or something along these lines.
If we took a more imaginative and bold approach to trying to resolve some of the problems of our youth, we would be much better off. It is the responsibility of parents and the people involved in dealing with youth-the educational system.
May 31, 1977

As the hon. members who have spoken so far have pointed out, it behooves the government to lay down the ground work and the framework on which we can deal with youth offenders.
As the law now stands, young offenders are dealt with under the Juvenile Delinquents Act of 1908, as amended from time to time. The act established special juvenile courts and special procedures for dealing with young offenders. Previously, young offenders had been treated as ordinary criminals and brought before the ordinary criminal courts. The intent of the 1908 act was to treat a child not as a criminal but as a misdirected child and one needing aid, encouragement, help and assistance. In view of the changes in society and how society has learned to deal with them, the 1908 act has not fulfilled its promise.
I would like to quote from the "Highlights of the Proposed New Legislation for Young Offenders" at page 1, which reads as follows:
In the view of many, young persons have not received proper care and treatment, and are not afforded all the basic rights and protections afforded to adults facing a criminal charge. It is also held that existing procedures fail to protect society and fail to bring about the salutary acceptance of responsibility for delinquent acts that should be part of the educational experience of the young offender.
Rather, the 1908 act with its concentration upon the offence of juvenile delinquency tends to label and stigmatize a child, thereby reinforcing a delinquent self-image and perpetuating delinquent behaviour.
The government has long recognized the need to replace the 1908 Juvenile Delinquents Act in an attempt to design better ways to deal with young persons who break the law and to reflect changes that have developed in the way young people are regarded in society. Its more recent efforts occurred in the fall of 1973 when cabinet authorized the Department of the Solicitor General and the Department of National Health and Welfare to carry out a joint review in consultation with provincial governments, of the programs, services and related financial arrangements concerning young persons in conflict with the law. The report of the federal-provincial joint review group, published in August of 1974, documented deficiencies in the juvenile justice field with respect to the limitations of present services and resources; the need for extensions of existing resources; and the need for federal-provincial assistance to extend existing resources to administer more adequately the present legislation.
Concurrent with the work of the federal-provincial joint review group, a committee on legislation was appointed by the Solicitor General with the view to submitting recommendations for new legislation to replace the Juvenile Delinquents Act. In September of 1975 the Solicitor General's committee on legislation released its report entitled "Young Persons in Conflict with the Law". The report was widely distributed across Canada for the express purpose of eliciting reactions, through consultation, from provincial government departments, from agencies and groups offering services to young persons in trouble, from professionals, interest groups and associations and the general public. In the year following the publication of the report approximately 70 meetings were held across the country, and over 150 briefs and submissions were received on the subject.
Criminal Code
The decision to organize and invest such time and resources in a wide reaching consultation process was a direct outcome of our past failures to bring about change in the field of juvenile justice in Canada. We are all familiar with the aborted attempts in the early seventies to replace the Juvenile Delinquents Act with Bill C-192, the young offenders legislation. It is generally agreed that one of the reasons for such failure was the lack of adequate consultation with interest groups and provincial governments prior to the presentation of the legislation to parliament.
For this reason, when the report on Young Persons in Conflict with the Law was released, the then solicitor general emphasized that before coming to final conclusions on new legislation it was important that consultation be undertaken to avoid the difficulties experienced with Bill C-192 and to provide for adequate public input on the development of legislation before proceeding to parliament.
At the close of the consultative process the reactions and suggested alternatives were closely analyzed, and a new set of legislative proposals was drafted. These proposals appeared in a document entitled "Highlights of the Proposed New Legislation for Young Offenders" which the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) tabled in the House of Commons on March 21 of this year.
The most recent legislative recommendations were discussed at the meeting of the continuing committee of deputy ministers of corrections in Regina on March 25 where responses to the proposed legislation were generally positive. The topic, particularly relating to a few specific outstanding issues, will also be discussed at the joint meeting of attorneys general and ministers responsible for corrections scheduled for the end of June.
The proposals for new legislation are aimed at incorporating changing principles and practices which have developed in the juvenile justice field over the years. In addition to formalizing such change, the proposals for new legislation create new processes and procedures to overcome the outdated features or inadequacies which exist in the Juvenile Delinquents Act. I would like to quote from "Highlights of the Proposed New Legislation for Young Offenders" as follows:
Young persons who commit offences should bear responsibility for their contraventions and while young persons should not in all instances be held accountable in the same manner or suffer the same consequences for their behaviour as adults, society must nonetheless be afforded the necessary protection from such illegal behaviour.
In affording society protection from illegal behaviour, it is to be recognized that young persons require supervision, discipline and control, but also, because of their state of dependency and lack of maturity, have special needs and require guidance and assistance.
Where not inconsistent with the protection of society, consideration should be given to using alternatives to the formal youth justice process for dealing with young persons who have committed offences which come within the jurisdiction of the Act.
In determining the responsibility of young persons under the Act, it is to be recognized that young persons have rights and freedoms equal to those of adults including those stated in the Canadian Bill of Rights; and in particular, a right to be heard in the course of, and to participate in, the processes that lead to
80016-48'/2

May 31, 1977
Criminal Code
decisions that affect them, as well as special guarantees of these rights and freedoms.
In the application of the Act, the rights of young persons include a right to the least interference with freedom, having regard to the protection of society, the needs of young persons, and the interests of their families.
Young persons have the right, in every instance where they have rights or freedoms which may be affected by the Act, to be informed as to what those rights and freedoms are.
Parents have primary responsibility for the care and supervision of their children and, therefore, young persons should be removed from parental supervision either partly or entirely only when all other measures that provide for continuing parental supervision are inappropriate; however, if it is necessary so to remove them, they shall be dealt with, in all respects and as nearly as may be, as they would be dealt with if they were under the care and protection of wise and conscientious parents.
Discussions and consultation during the past three years have not, however, been restricted to the substance of legislation, as I have just outlined. A major objective has been to identify the resource requirements and financial implications of new legislation and to explore ways of extending additional federal financial support to the juvenile justice system.
As a result of our detailed discussions the federal government is now prepared to extend the range of juvenile services eligible for cost sharing to include diversion services, pre-dispositional assessments and reports, and post-dispositional community supervision, including probation. Such additional funding assistance would be extended under the framework of the proposed social services legislation.
These additional services place greater reliance on community solutions to the problems of young offenders are distinct from current financial assistance to provinces for custodial services which remove a young person from his home and often from his community.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR STATISTICAL DATA INDICATING RISK OF OIL SPILLS AS RESULT OF INCREASED TANKER TRAFFIC
TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR STATISTICAL DATA INDICATING RISK OF OIL SPILLS AS RESULT OF INCREASED TANKER TRAFFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my questions to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), which were really a series of questions initiated on May 19 and continued on May 20 last, were to ask the minister whether he, or his department, was in a position to table in the House statistical data, or a report containing statistical data, which would indicate the risk factor in connection with the marine handling of oil and other hazardous cargo.
These questions were prompted by two recent events, the first of which was the release of a report commissioned by the Department of Fisheries and the Environment which was made available to those members of parliament who were interested. The report was entitled "The Determination of Probabilities of Oil Spills in Canadian Arctic Waters" and dealt specifically with the probabilities of blowouts in exploratory drilling in the Beaufort Sea and other Arctic areas. The briefing note from the environmental protection service of the department which accompanied the report indicated:
May 31, 1977

The report is an application to off-shore exploratory drilling of a method used to evaluate nuclear reactor safety. It uses the laws of probability to combine the probabilities of basic events which could lead to a blowout so as to predict the probability of a blowout.
The briefing note then goes on to say that while the report is limited,
... the report in its present form provides the best available statistical basis for decision-making.
My position is that it is very difficult as an issue to separate exploratory drilling from the handling of hazardous cargo. It may be that if we are successful in exploratory drilling, the amount of oil tanker traffic would dramatically increase, and therefore these two issues are inextricably combined.
The second event that prompted my series of questions to the Minister of Transport was a document filed by that department entitled "National Marine Emergency Plan" which deals with our capabilities, among other things, of handling oil spills and other toxic materials. I immediately had to ask myself that, given this report, which I found to be an interesting and informative report, does the department know the probability of an oil spill or of the spill of other toxic material and, if it does not, how can one evaluate the efficacy of the report or the ability to handle clean-up operations?
On May 20 when I asked the minister the second set of questions he indicated that internal working documents were available to him and that the department was developing positions in anticipation of an international conference. Therefore 1 have to ask if the department is in a position to make domestic decisions in this regard. Certainly they went so far as to file this marine emergency plan, and if they are in a position to adopt a Canadian position at what would presumably be an important international conference, why can they not table the material in the House of Commons? In my view his answer is unsatisfactory.
We are dealing daily with increased tanker traffic, super tankers, marine traffic and other hazardous cargo, super ports, such as the one that exists at Cherry Point, Washington, and the proposed Kitimat super-port on the west coast. Why in this area, when we have reports on nuclear reactor risks, on exploratory drilling risks, and a report from the Department of Fisheries and the Environment entitled "An Environmental Risk Index for the Siting of Deep Water Oil Ports", do we not have the report on the risk of handling oil and other hazardous cargo? I would like to know what the risk would be with increased traffic of oil tankers and other cargo ships, what it would be with increased size of ships, in certain weather conditions and at certain times of the year, all of which can be done actuarially.
To my dismay I found I could write or phone the U.S. coastguard and secure information from them, and yet we are in a position here in Canada where the minister can make a decision on the Canadian position at an international conference and yet is not in a position to table the material on which he based the decision. I can only assume therefore that the government maintains the view that this information is so
Adjournment Debate
technical that it should not be made available to the public for fear they would misunderstand, or not understand it at all. I suggest, in reply to that paranoia, that the government greatly underestimates the maturity of the Canadian public and the maturity of this House. How else can we make proper decisions-except of course the NDP who are always inclined to throw out the matter whether it be Kitimat or the Makenzie Valley or anything else-and how can we act responsibly and responsively unless the Minister of Transport is willing to take us into his confidence and release this information to us?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR STATISTICAL DATA INDICATING RISK OF OIL SPILLS AS RESULT OF INCREASED TANKER TRAFFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to answer a part of my distinguished colleague's question in the three minutes available to me. I am sure he understands and appreciates that it will be difficult to do so in three minutes.
The main source of the vessel casualty statistics used in developing an oil spill expectation analysis for Canadian ship terminal systems was provided through records of the 3,763 world-wide tanker accidents which took place between 19691974. Records included only those tankers which have greater than 3,000 tons deadweight, which excluded, therefore, small harbour tankers used for bunkering ships in port.
An oil spill expectation algorithm was then developed from these existing ship casualty statistics in conjunction with predicted change in the volume of the marine traffic flow within the ship terminal system under consideration. Further, the algorithm was modified to encompass all the marine network constraints of the ship terminal system, including critical channel widths and areas of concern.
As you might appreciate, Mr. Speaker, some fairly complicated calculations are required to arrive at an algorithm which would take into account such factors as spill probability for coastal and ship terminal areas, exposure rates of design ships, etc., but time this afternoon does not allow me to pursue these factors in more depth.
Now, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the Kitimat ship terminal oil spill expectations, using this algorithm it was concluded that over a 25-year period there is a 75 per cent probability of one pollution causing incident of a major nature developing within the Kitimat ship terminal system, which could cause an oil outflow of 387 tons. In addition, an annual oil outflow of approximately 35 tons arising from minor incidents could be expected.
In conclusion I should like to point out that these oil spill tonnages compare favourably with the empirical rule of 40-70 barrels spill expected per million barrels of oil throughput.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-EFFECT OF PROPOSED TAKE-OVER OF TRANSAIR BY PACIFIC WESTERN ON PRAIRIE REGIONAL SERVICE
AIR TRANSPORT-EFFECT OF PROPOSED TAKE-OVER OF TRANSAIR BY PACIFIC WESTERN ON PRAIRIE REGIONAL SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 6 I asked a question regarding the long anticipated prairie air service. It was one of a series of questions I have asked since 1974 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in

May 31, 1977
Adjournment Debate
company with the then minister of national defence, the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson), made a special trip to Winnipeg. He announced, during the election campaign, that there would be a prairie air service commenced, and that it would be dealt with expeditiously because it was realized that first-class air service was necessary to the continuing progress of the economy and of the community of eastern Saskatchewan and western Manitoba.
There has been no action since that time in specific terms other than a long series of negotiations, changes of mind, and unkept promises. This evening I raise the issue again in the hope, now that another summer is upon us, that we will be able to get assurance that this long anticipated service will commence during the summer months of 1977. I say this because it will require certain upgrading of facilities, and in answer to questions the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has indicated that plans are under way and the necessary infrastructure will proceed as soon as the decision is made.
The situation becomes more ridiculous when you realize that in 1973 a terminal was opened at the airport just north of Brandon, Manitoba, which cost a considerable sum of money, and a short time later the service was withdrawn. This only adds to the urgency of the matter.
We thought we were about to get an air service when negotiations were under way with the province of Manitoba. But the proposal was turned down because it proved unsatisfactory to the government and the Minister of Transport. The minister has stated specifically that he wants commuter service between Winnipeg, Yorkton and Saskatoon. He has offered a $.9 million subsidy for that purpose. He also wants a jet service between Toronto, Brandon and Regina, and is providing a $1.1 million subsidy for that purpose.
A further complication emerged recently. As was indicated in the press and statements in this House, Pacific Western Airlines is now negotiating with Transair to take-over that facility and develop a co-ordinated and organized western regional air service. Transair has made the specific proposal in response to the minister's subsidy proposals. When I askeu the question on May 6 the minister indicated that the last date for intervention was May 9, after which the Canadian Transport Commission would decide. Almost three weeks have passed since that date, and I hope this evening that whoever speaks for the government will indicate that the green signal has been given, that the service has been announced, and that we will receive the good news soon. We hope that at long last this badly needed air service will be provided to the prairie region and that the service will be well under way this summer.
I raise another matter in connection with the anticipated Pacific Western Airlines take-over of Transair. We want several assurances in this regard. As was indicated, negotiations will take almost one year. The government has approved the conducting of the negotiations. We want the assurance that the Transair maintenance base will remain in Winnipeg. Air Canada's moving its base to Montreal created an economic

disaster of considerable proportions. That disaster was slowly being put right by the establishment of a maintenance air base operated by Transair. I hope we shall have the assurance that this facility will remain, despite the proposed take-over by Pacific Western Airlines.
We also want the assurance that jet service is still an essential part of the minister's proposal. If it will not be possible for a western regional air carrier to provide this service, we want the assurance that Air Canada will discharge that obligation. We used to have Air Canada service. That, unfortunately, was discontinued. Air Canada could easily divert one of its jets to the Toronto-Brandon-Regina route.
First and foremost, we trust the government can indicate this evening that the service will begin this coming summer.

subtopic: INCOME TAX-MEAL ALLOWANCE FOR TRUCK DRIVERS- POSSIBILITY OF CHANGE
INCOME TAX-MEAL ALLOWANCE FOR TRUCK DRIVERS- POSSIBILITY OF CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a number of hourly wage earners in my constituency. A good many of them are truck drivers. Some of them have come to me with a problem that is endemic to the trucking industry. The Income Tax Department requires daily receipts for all meals which the truckers eat. In consequence of their representations, I asked the minister a question on March 22, which stated in part:
May 31, 1977

As the minister is aware, many of these drivers spend up to 200 days a year in their cabs, which is not the most conducive place to conduct office procedure, yet they are allowed only $7.50 per day for meals without receipts, whereas members of her department receive an allowance of up to $15. Is there any plan in her department or on her part to change the present requirement for truck drivers and allow at least $12 per day?
The first thing I would like to point out regarding this policy is the fact that it is discriminatory. Truckers have to show receipts in the 1975 taxation year for anything spent beyond $7.50. I understand it has now been increased to $9. By and large, what the tax department is saying is that they will grant them as little as possible without receipts.
Federal employees who travel on behalf of the government outside of their offices are granted per diems with no receipts at as realistic a rate as possible of at least $13.50 or $15. I do not understand why a truck driver should only get half as much an allowance as a civil servant.
These truckers travel across the country. They cannot just stop at any old place and get a meat that is good for them. They are hard working men and they deserve a little bit of allowance.
The minister said in a letter to me that it is a matter of control, the department has to be able to control expense. I received a notification from a hotel owner in an interior city. He pointed out that most federal civil servants when they stay outside the main metropolitan area go to a hotel down the street where they pay $22 or $23 a night, whereas if they stay at another hotel or motel they could get the same accommodation for $14 or $16. 1 do not think the government is in any position to talk about control over spending. The only ones it wants to control are the wage earners.
The second point I want to make is that the whole procedure of requiring these receipts is uneconomic. Imagine a tax file being delivered to the Income Tax office containing the records of a truck driver on the road for 200 days, eating three meals a day, with a total of 600 receipts. An accountant in the office would have to total the 600 receipts. If he missed a few, he would have to look through them again. He would have to be paid wages while counting those receipts. At the end, his figure may be challenged by the taxpayer and he would have to do it again. On the difference between the $7.50 and the $9, or the $9 and the $12 the truck drivers would like to have, when you figure out the tax on that difference is it an economic procedure to have a civil servant totalling all of those receipts, maybe twice, and then figuring out the difference? They might save a couple of bucks, but they will get it off the blue collar workers.
The third point I want to make is that this is a very disturbing mentality on the part of the government. Essentially what the government is saying is that every truck driver in this country is a potential crook. The government feels he should be watched because he might eat more than $9 worth of food. If he happened to have $11 or $12, the government might miss out on 30 cents. Therefore it tries to get that crook.
I lived in the United States for a few years. I attended university and worked part time there. I had to file an income
Adjournment Debate
tax return. The difference I saw was this. Any time I had to File an income tax claim in the United States I could go to that office and I could say, "Look, here is my file, can you help me with it?" And they would say, "Sure, here are two or three other places where you can save some money; you did not make the deductions for it." But try to do that with the Canadian revenue service. They would say, "You are trying to get away with something here." It is an entirely different attitude in Canada. What we are doing is educating our people to see themselves as potential crooks. Why cannot we give them the benefit of the doubt and let them eat proper meals on the road, quit fudging on a few receipts, and let them feel as though they were upstanding, honourable, taxpaying, working people?
The irony is that according to an article in the Vancouver Sun, when prisoners are let out of our penitentiaries on compassionate leave they are allowed $15. But a truck driver gets $9. I guess crime pays. Salesmen, when they go on the road, can take their customers to lunch. They can buy them cocktails, get them rib steaks, give them liqueurs. It is all a deductible expense. But unless a truck driver takes his three meals at McDonald's he will be seen as a crook if he does not have receipts.
I know one taxpayer who went to the bother of saving all his receipts for three months just to prove to the taxation department that he was spending $12 a day on meals. Mr. Speaker, you have been on trains. You know what it costs to eat on the road. A working man needs three square meals a day. Yet this gentleman who saved his receipts and proved beyond a doubt that after three months he had spent $12 a day was told, at the end, "Give us the receipts for the other nine months or you don't get your deduction."

subtopic: INCOME TAX-MEAL ALLOWANCE FOR TRUCK DRIVERS- POSSIBILITY OF CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the administrative procedures insofar as away-from-home expenses are concerned are explained in detail in our information circular 73-21R2. The hon. member asked about the allowance for meals for long-distance truck drivers for income tax purposes. An employee of a trucking company or other employer whose principal business is goods and passenger transport, and is required regularly to travel away from his home terminal on vehicules used by his employer for that purpose, may deduct amounts disbursed for meals and lodging while travelling to the extent he is not entitled to be reimbursed by his employer.
He may claim under one of two procedures. Under the simplified method, he may file with his tax return a listing of trips actually taken, and the department will allow a maximum cost of $3.00 per meal without a supporting voucher. Under the detailed method, the employee must maintain a record book in which each disbursement is recorded, including the name and location of the restaurant and individual amounts expended. Disbursements so recorded will be allowed to the

May 31, 1977
Export Development Act
extent they are reasonable and where they are in excess of $3 a meal they must be supported by vouchers.
Some members may quarrel with this method but it seems to me the simplest and the easiest way. We all recognize that in parts of the country it may not be possible to get a reasonable meal for $3. All we ask a person to do is to collect his bills and to list them.
Anyone who can live within the $3 meal ticket has an easy job; he does not have to collect any receipts. The hon. member referred to salesmen or executives taking their clients out for luxurious meals and deducting the cost from their income tax. Obviously in that case receipts must be collected; I do not think there is any other way. The idea of the $3 meal is to make it easy for those who eat a quick hamburger lunch. For those who want to taste French cuisine, we simply ask them to collect receipts so they can deduct the cost.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE THE MAXIMUM LIABILITY OF THE CORPORATION AND CREDIT GUARANTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I called it five o'clock I was speaking about the Export Develop-

ment Corporation and its treatment of those who have small claims. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) illustrated the point and spoke about the large amounts which were going to be lent to corporations to develop and to build companies in foreign countries which might even be competing against us because of their lower labour costs. That is the point I had come to when I called it five o'clock.
I want to deal with the question of how the little fellow- Small Industry- is treated in this regard. I have a claim here before me which goes back to August 3 of 1971. At that time I believe the minister of industry, trade and commerce was the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie). At that time there was a shipment of 40 bazoos made to the buyer on the terms of DOP/SD, later revised to 50 per cent 90 days, 50 per cent 150 days. That was the contract. On December 21, 1971, EDC was notified by Otaco Limited about the damaged condition of some goods which had arrived. I am just following this sequence and putting it on the record, and I will have more to say on each one individually.
On November 7, 1972, Otaco's representatives visited EDC and notified EDC that a claim was being placed with the Marine Insurance Company. EDC advised Otaco to send a representative to Kenya to sort out the problem. On January 19, 1973, the commercial secretary of the Canadian High Commission at Nairobi, Kenya, telexed Otaco suggesting that a representative from Otaco visit Kenya to sort out Marine Insurance problems and legal positions. On January 26, 1973, EDC advised Otaco that nothing had been heard from them since the meeting of November 7, 1972. Otaco wrote EDC suggesting that a representative from EDC visit Kenya with Otaco's sales manager. EDC advised Otaco that a trip to Kenya by a representative from EDC would not be justified at that time. Hon. members must realize that with all the contacts EDC and the government must have in Kenya, that type of answer should not have been given to a firm in Ontario.
On February 26, 1973, a claim was placed with EDC for the amount owing to Otaco by Grafton Construction Company. On March 21, 1973, EDC again advised Otaco that Otaco should send a representative to Kenya but that EDC could not consider paying the claim until the dispute regarding the damaged goods was settled. That claim was settled by the insurance company, yet EDC never kept its end of the bargain, nor did the minister and neither did the minister see that EDC kept its end of the bargain in this matter.
I would like to go back to the rules of the game as they are laid down. When goods are delivered in good condition they should be paid for, or if the people who order them go bankrupt, they should still be paid for. This is a part of that policy:
... failure of the buyer to pay ... goods delivered to and accepted by the buyer. . . .failure or refusal of the buyer to accept the goods .. . where such failure is not excused by and does not arise from . .. any breach of contract on the part of the exporter. . . insolvency of the buyer...
The buyer went broke in this situation and was unable to pay, and yet that firm was made to make good the loan at the bank for those bazoos. This contract was entered into, and the
May 31, 1977

claim is claim number 3354. This contract was entered into by the Grafton Construction Company to buy 40 units of bazoos. A bazoo is an all terrain vehicle. It can go on land, water, mud or sand. It is an all purpose vehicle. Those units were sold to the Grafton Construction Company of Nairobi, Kenya. The goods were delivered and marked "Notify Bantam Plant Sales Company Limited". From all of the lengthy correspondence, I was able to learn from the government or its representative in Nairobi what part the Bantam sales organization played in this transaction.
I learned that the Bantam sales organization was to assemble the vehicles. The buyer was the Grafton Construction Company Limited. When the goods were inspected, it was found that some of the crates were damaged as well as some of the bazoos. The crates were landed at Mombasa and placed in bond. The Grafton Construction Company accepted the documents. The insurance company paid for the damaged goods. The insurance company accepted the claim, and for the goods which were damaged it paid $10,000. Surely that was evidence that the goods were all there and accepted. The insurance company accepted the claim, but the Export Development Corporation would not accept it. That left $30,000 still owed by this company.
The claim was pressed, and there was various correspondence. This went on from 1971 to December, 1975, when the last letter was filed, a period covering four years. I want to say to everyone in this House that expensive bureaucracy was never more demonstrated than it was in this little claim for $30,000 which that small firm had to pay. It cost 13 men their jobs. I am illustrating this case because we were talking about big deals involving other corporations amounting to millions of dollars over 15 years. This matter extended over a period of five years. Over and over the minister stated that he was working on it to see what could be done.
The rules which are laid down plainly provide that the Export Development Corporation will reimburse a firm which goes broke, if it bought goods. The company was assured of this at the bank, but who paid? This little firm paid and, as I said, 13 people lost their jobs. Another firm bought this firm out. I say again that the minister should consider this and see that the little guy gets a fair deal. The machines which were built would have been of tremendous help in Kenya where the terrain goes from mud to lakes to streams to rivers, and so forth. Bazoos can go across all of those things. This equipment was needed.
I have a whole file of correspondence here. I only read part of it. I do not intend to put it all on the record. However, I want to say that the auditors in Kenya checked the books and found everything to be in order. Why did they go to all that trouble never to pay that claim? Why all this bureaucracy?
I think it is time we took a look at the bureaucracy we have today and are developing in this country at taxpayer's expense. In this case $30,000 was involved. Two or three trips by the bureaucracy on its expensive aircraft could have been taken, the whole thing could have been paid on the expense incurred on investigation, it could have been written off and EDC could
Judges Act
have kept its word because the insurance company paid the claim.
I am appealing for a square deal not just for multinational corporations, for corporations which are going to borrow millions of dollars over a long period of years, and not for communist countries which are lent money at low rates of interest. I am appealing for small companies in Canada that hire Canadian workmen. They should be looked after on a small claim such as this just as attentively as a big corporation is looked after, as the hon. member for York-Simcoe said today, a company which may be establishing in some foreign country and which will compete with us because of the lower wage scale there. That is my point, and I hope the minister has listened attentively to the case of the little worker who, for five or six years, went through the wringer of bureaucracy and in the final analysis was cheated.

During the debate on second reading of this bill I spoke of the importance of preserving, and indeed, enhancing the independence of the judiciary. I indicated that this is a responsibility resting equally upon the government, the legislators, and the judiciary itself.
In this bill there are a number of provisions directed to this end. Provision is made for the appointment of a number of additional judges to enable the courts to contend with increasing case loads. Modest salary increases for judges are authorized to maintain judicial salaries at appropriate levels. Further representational allowances and conference allowances are provided to enable judges to keep abreast of developments in the law and to discharge special duties attaching to their offices.
In particular, there are the provisions creating a new regime for the administration of federal judicial affairs and establishing a county court committee of the Canadian Judicial Council.
As proposed in the legislation, the transfer from the Department of Justice to the new commissioner for federal judicial affairs, who is to be appointed only after consultation with the Canadian Judicial Council, that is to say, after consultation with the Chief Justice of Canada and the chief justices of appeal and of the superior courts in all the provinces and to the registrar of the Supreme Court of Canada of responsibility for the administrative affairs of federally appointed judges and federally constituted courts is a significant step forward in enhancing the judiciary's independence. It also recognizes the singular importance of the Supreme Court of Canada as the apex of our judicial system.
The creation of the county court committee equally strengthens the Canadian judicial council which was established in 1971 as a forum in which the judiciary itself could assume direct and active responsibility for enhancing the efficiency, quality, and uniformity of judicial services and for the self-discipline of judges throughout Canada. The Committee will provide an opportunity for the county and district

court judges to participate more actively and directly in a number of the council's affairs.
Consequently, passage of this bill will constitute another important step in affirming parliament's commitment to the principle of an independent judiciary, and I wish to commend and thank members of this House who, both during second reading debate and committee consideration of this bill, gave close consideration to the measures provided for in the bill, and who also assisted in ensuring early passage of it by the House.
