speakeroldname: Mr. Eldon M. Woolliams (Calgary North) moved:
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
That Bill C-25, an act to extend the present laws in Canada that proscribe discrimination and that protect the privacy of individuals, be amended in Clause 43, by adding immediately after line 4 at page 25 the following new subclause:
(3) Notwithstanding this Act, or any other Act of the Parliament of
Canada, an appeal shall lie to a Federal Court of Canada from any order or
decision or review of a tribunal, or from any dismissal of a complaint by a
tribunal
(a)	on any ground of appeal involving a question of law;
(b)	on any ground of appeal involving a question of mixed law and fact;
(c)	on any ground of appeal involving a question of fact.
He said: Mr. Speaker, may I say that I moved this amendment in committee but we have not received the committee report yet. I would have liked to have seen what was said by all members of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and to have incorporated some of their remarks in the record. I felt I had the sympathy of members of the committee on all sides. All came to me-I am not breaking any confidence in saying this and I shall not name them but I can say
Canadian Human Rights
that some are smiling now as they look at me-and said they were concerned that there was no appeal.
In my experience at the bar, Mr. Speaker, once there has been a finding of fact by the trial judge, tribunal or administrative body, and providing they have acted within the law and have not usurped the principle of natural justice or waived jurisdiction by some irregularity, and if there is no appeal from the facts, then the decision handed down stands.
I have had some experience with the Federal Court Act, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to read Section 18 into the record. It reads as follows:
The Trial Division has exclusive original jurisdiction ...
The Federal Court was set up to deal with most matters that relate to the federal statutes. There is one exception, however.
I see the minister looking at me and I will tell him what that exception is. I have had experience with it. Under the Broadcasting Act you can apply to any superior court in the province. That is much better than having to go to the Federal Court because few lawyers understand that the rules and regulations are more in tune with the British system than with the Canadian system in the Federal Court.
Section 18 continues as follows:
(a)	to issue an injunction, writ of certiorari, writ of prohibition, writ of mandamus or writ of quo warranto, or grant declaratory relief, against any federal board, commission or other tribunal; and
(b)	to hear and determine any application or other proceeding for relief in the nature of relief contemplated by paragraph (a), including any proceeding brought against the Attorney General of Canada, to obtain relief against a federal board, commission or other tribunal.
Section 18 deals with special damages. A writ of certiorari is where there has been a mistake on the record or a mistake in law; where jurisdiction has been exceeded it can be quashed by procedures. If some person acts beyond their jurisdiction then there is a writ of prohibition. If some administrator will not do what he is supposed to do, there is a writ of mandamus.
I know what the minister is going to say. He will say that this is good legislation that is on the books and that we do not need any procedure of appeal under the Human Rights Act.
Section 28 of the Federal Court Act is quite broad. It reads as follows:
(1) Notwithstanding section 18 or the provisions of any other Act, the Court of Appeal has jurisdiction-
That is the appeal court of the Federal Court. It continues:
-to hear and determine an application to review and set aside a decision or order, other than a decision or order of an administrative nature-
I want the House, and particularly the lawyers here, to listen to that again:
-other than a decision or order of an administrative nature-
Some boards and tribunals-and I will deal with them when 1 deal with the Human Rights Act-make administrative orders and make decisions of an administrative nature.
In committee the minister said that this is sufficient and that we do not have to worry but, Mr. Speaker, I can quote many cases, and if it is of an administrative nature you might just as well forget about any appeal under the act.

May 31, 1977
Canadian Human Rights Section 28 continues:
-not required by law to be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis, made by or in the course of proceedings before a federal board, commission or other tribunal, upon the ground that the board, commission or tribunal (a) failed to observe a principle of natural justice or otherwise acted beyond or refused to exercise its jurisdiction;
I read again:
(a)	failed to observe a principle of natural justice or otherwise acted beyond or refused to exercise its jurisdiction;
That is a question of law.
(b)	erred in law in making its decision or order, whether or not the error appears on the face of the record; or
(c)	based its decision or order on an erroneous finding of fact that it made in a perverse or capricious manner or without regard for the material before it.
No matter what the minister may say, Section 28 gives the right of appeal to an individual from the decision of an administrative tribunal only on a question of law. Consider the wording of subparagraph (c) " .. . based its decision or order on an erroneous finding of fact." That language refers to a judge's finding something as a fact where there was no evidence to support such finding; or that he found something as a fact, totally contrary to the evidence. The subparagraph goes on to-say, "-that it made in a perverse or capricious manner-". That language refers to a perverse or capricious finding of fact.
As the minister well knows, there is lots of law saying that a perverse finding of fact involves a question of law. Therefore, the only right of appeal under the Federal Court Act is on a question of law.
I now come to my amendment. It asks that, notwithstanding this act or any other act of the Parliament of Canada, an appeal shall lie to a federal court from any order or decision, on any ground of appeal involving a question of law. That language does not contradict the language of the act. Subparagraph (b) reads: "On any ground of appeal involving a question of mixed law and fact." That point can cause difficulty. What is a question of mixed law and fact? I suggest it would include a perverse finding of fact. The last part of my proposed amendment reads, "(c) on any ground of appeal involving a question of fact."
This evening we are considering Bill C-25, an act to extend the present laws in Canada that proscribe discrimination and that protect the privacy of individuals. In other words, we are considering a human rights bill.
Before I get to the meat of my argument allow me to read Clause 2 of the bill. It says:
The purpose of this Act is to extend the present laws in Canada to give effect, within the purview of matters coming within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, to the following principles:
(a) every individual should have an equal opportunity with other individuals to make for himself or herself the life that he or she is able and wishes to have, consistent with his or her duties and obligations as a member of society, without being hindered in or prevented from doing so by discriminatory practices based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex or marital status, or conviction for an offence for which a pardon has been 
granted or by discriminatory employement practices based on physical handicap; and
b) the privacy of individuals should be protected to the greatest extent
consistent with public order and well-being.
The intent of that language is almost identical to the intent of the language in the Bill of Rights. Both pieces of legislation will commend themselves to Canadians. Elowever, when you analyze this bill you will note that a tribunal is to be set up, or a commission, and one person can make a decision. What will be the effect of this? Let me give an example.
I have many friends in Calgary, some of them Jewish. One of those people owned a shop a little way from my office. When my children were younger I used to stop at his shop on the way home and buy my kids a little candy and popcorn. We always used to chat about politics. This chap hired, let us say, a Pakistani, and for some unknown reason some people of the community did not like the person he hired. They kept throwing bricks through his window. He had been at that location for 35 years and never encountered trouble. What happened?
Finally, he said to his employee, "Look, I feel sorry for you; we have suffered from discrimination, and you are suffering from it also. All the same, I am afraid I will have to let you go, because nobody will insure my windows. The people of this area are heaving bricks through them almost every night".
What would happen if his employee were to take his case to the human rights tribunal, if this bill were law? I assume this bill will pass. Say one man hears the case and says to my little friend, whom I have known 35 years, "You discriminated against your worker, you fired him because he was of a certain race. We do not know who is throwing the bricks, but I say to you, rehire that man. If you do not, we will close your shop or remove your popcorn machine." This could happen under this human rights bill.
Let us say this happens, as I have recited it, and my little friend loses his popcorn machine and is forced to close down the business he has operated 35 years. Unless this bill is amended, on those facts my little friend would have no right of appeal, because the tribunal say there is no question of law involved and, "I find you have discriminated against Mr. X," whatever the employee's name might be. Mr. Speaker, I am shocked that lawyers in this House and elsewhere have not been up in arms about this provision.
Hearing my submission in committee, the minister, showing either good judgment or political acumen, decided that yes, something must be done in relation to such arbitrary decisions. He said, "I tell you what; I agree that one man on a tribunal might make a mistake. Therefore let us make available the right of appeal." The aggrieved person, if less than three sit on the original tribunal, can appeal to other tribunal members, but these will all be administrators, appointed by order in council, and very likely all Liberals.

speechtext:

This will be without a right of appeal on facts because 99 per cent of the judgments, providing they are acting within the scope of their jurisdiction as a board, if it can sit as one man, are on findings of fact.
I think I know some law. Hon. members flattered me this afternoon. Tonight they will criticize me. That is typical of this place. How can one person make a mistake on law when under the act he has a right to find the facts? Once he finds the facts, that is the decision. You can check Sections 18 or 28 of the Federal Act and you will see there is no right of appeal.
Once I appealed to the legal instinct of the Minister of Justice. He said that maybe he had made a mistake, and he repented. When the Minister of Justice repents, it is quite a repentance. He said "We will allow you to appeal to your friends." It goes to the same old board, the same old club that belongs to the same group. That is no appeal at all.
We are dealing with human rights. Any individual, whether it be an employer, employee or unemployed person should have the right of appeal. The Minister of Justice does not agree.
In the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, we live together. We flatter each other. We are lawyers. We see eyeball to eyeball. I have been a member of that committee for quite a while. But there is one thing I have learned over the years. Once the government decides to do something, it does it.
This bill was not drawn up by the minister. He probably did not see it until it came to his office. It was drawn by a bunch
Canadian Human Rights
of bureaucrats. However, he has to justify it. I will tell you why. If he goes against those who tell him what to do, do you know what happens? They have a little discussion over coffee. They say that the minister is acting rather queer, going against what they are doing. He therefore has to stay within the terms of reference of his department. If we were the government, I guess we would have to do the same thing. However, that does not mean that I cannot raise the kind of grievance I am raising now.
Surely the minister is not going to tell me that the commissioners appointed to that tribunal will be perfect, great men who never have any ideas. Why does the government deny my amendment? What is it afraid of? I will tell you. What government supporters fear most is that once they set up this administrative body they do not want any interference. According to Sections 18 and 28 of the federal act, there is no right of appeal from a finding of fact. Ninety percent of the decisions made by administrative boards, superior trial courts and county courts are on findings of fact.
There is a judge in Alberta who is now retired, God bless him. He was so frightened of an appeal from his judgments that whoever he would find for, the plaintiff for example, he would say, "I believe the plaintiff and disbelieve the witnesses for the defence. These are the facts."
The Court of Appeal would know it was a perverse finding. However, because of the law there could be no appeal from a finding of fact because trial judges are able to find those facts on the evidence. They would look at the witnesses and, when making their decisions, they would say who was telling the truth and who was not. Therefore the appeal would be thrown out of the court.

In my own province there were trial judges so shaped and trimmed in their understanding of that kind of jurisprudence they could make a finding of fact against you that you could win in the court of appeal in Alberta. However, the Supreme Court of Canada followed the British practice and upset the judgment of the court of appeal. They always reinstated the original judgment.
We had a judge who is now retired, a great gentleman. I will not name him. He never wrote a judgment. If he was going to find for the plaintiff in an automobile accident, he would say "I find negligence. I give the plaintiff $50,000 and costs and double column five". Mr. Speaker, I listened transfixed to the speech made by my hon. friend from Calgary North. The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yew-chuk) said it was the best speech of the day. He spoke with eloquence. He spoke with conviction, he spoke from a long background in the practice of the law, and 1 think he brought home as forcefully as anyone could in this House the importance of distinguishing in our jurisprudence between an administrative tribunal with judicial overtones and the judiciary itself.
There is in practice and in fact a difference between an administrative tribunal on the one hand, however well inten-tioned its members may be, and the traditions which surround the judges and our courts. I join with the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) in appealing to the minister and to the government to consider the amendment which has been put on the order paper. I would remind the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) if I can do so, with the greatest respect, that this is the first time that there has been a human rights bill of this magnitude covering the matters which this bill covers within the federal jurisdiction.
Listen to part of Clause 2. It says:
(a)	every individual should have an equal opportunity with other individuals to make for himself or herself the life that he or she is able and wishes to have, consistent with his or her duties and obligations as a member of society, without being hindered in or prevented from doing so by discriminatory practices based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex or marital status, or conviction for an offence for which a pardon has been granted or by discriminatory employment practices based on physical handicap; and
(b)	the privacy of individuals should be protected to the greatest extent consistent with public order and well-being.
I do not intend to stand in this House and denigrate the sentiments of the minister with respect to this bill because it is one which affects every one of our lives. Yesterday in this House I raised the case of a person who feels discriminated against because of colour. I would not want that person's future to be decided on the basis of an arbitrary decision within the bureaucracy, however well intentioned, and I would not want to see that man denied access to the courts of this country. If that recourse were denied to him he would harbour within his soul for the rest of his days the suspicion that he had not been fairly dealt with.
I say to the minister that this is the first attempt, and a noble attempt indeed, to bring within our jurisdiction, at least at the federal level, some recognition of equality among individuals before the law regardless of their station. What is so wrong if that is the case? What is so wrong with acceding to
May 31, 1977

what my hon. friend from Calgary North has asked, and allowing those who must deal with this tribunal in one way or another, at least at the beginning while we test this new system, the right which has been granted historically, as it ought to have been granted, that is, access to the courts?
The amendment is broad, but the principles with which we are dealing are broad and, as I say, it will affect all of us in one way or another. This is the government's first attempt. The hon. member for Calgary North is absolutely right. Even within the judicial process there are occasions when people walk away from the courtroom feeling aggrieved. It is pretty hard to tell a person, as I have had to from time to time, why they lost their case. It is hard to get them to understand why, in a matter involving dollars and cents, or freedom, or relations between individuals, the court has found the facts against them and that another court cannot deal with the facts. In the mind of that person that is dreadfully wrong. It is no comfort for him to be told that had there been an error in law there would be a chance to go to another court and appear before a different set of judges.
We are not talking here about matters of dollars and cents or about relations between individuals. We are talking about the relationship between society and individuals. This is why the hon. member for Calgary North has gone so far in his amendment as to deal not only with errors in law which are to be the subject of appeal, and which I hope is nothing unusual, but errors involving mixed law and fact as well as errors involving a question of fact.
In this first attempt we are making to legislate broadly in the field of human rights we are saying to the people of this country that we have done our very best to ensure that all avenues are kept open to them, that no one avenue has been closed. If the amendment does not pass, then in terms of this new approach to that which human beings normally take for granted-the relationship of one individual to another, fairness of society and a whole host of other things-we will be saying that such matters ought not to be a matter for the court.
I appeal to the Minister of Justice to reconsider his position overnight on this matter. I am sure he has received representations from members of his own party on this subject. I cannot imagine some members from his own party on the committee, for all of whom I have great respect, not making representations to him privately in regard to this provision. I ask him to consider those representations as well as those put forward by the hon. member for Calgary North. I do not want this bill to leave this parliament deficient. I want the bill to leave this parliament as complete a first step as it possibly can be. I am afraid that unless there is couched within the bill those provisions suggested by the hon. member for Calgary North in his amendment, then the bill will be deficient and the government will have reason to regret its failure to support this amendment.
I am not suggesting that it would not be other than an administrative inconvenience to have an extra ground of

appeal. I am not suggesting that there would not be some delay. But it would be a delay occasioned by people who felt themselves legitimately aggrieved by a decision. I think it important that we not let administrative inconvenience stand in the way of the proper administration of justice.
The Minister of Justice has talked from time to time about the two roles he performs. As Minister of Justice he has administrative responsibility for a department of government. He is also the Attorney General of Canada, which puts him above party. It puts him above considerations of mere convenience. It puts him in the position where he has to consider the administration of justice in a way perhaps different from any other member of the House of Commons.
It is in that spirit that I am happy to support this amendment which is being so ably presented by the hon. member for Calgary North. Mr. Speaker, I am glad to rise and support my friend, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) in the amendment he has moved at the report stage of Bill C-25. As my hon. friend from Calgary North so ably pointed out, how can you start to define in a proper way human rights when in the interpretation clause of the bill legal rights are denied or restricted? In terms of the new area which this bill reaches into trying to remove discrimination of various forms, it is rather ironic, to say the least, that in attempting to control or eliminate discrimination the bill takes away something which has been fundamental in almost every bill, namely, the right of appeal to a higher tribunal.
I agree with my hon. friend from Grenville-Carleton that undoubtedly if this amendment were carried an appeal to the Federal Court might occasion delay. But, Mr. Speaker, what is a little delay in terms of defining human rights and making sure that errors are corrected when, on the other side of the coin, there could very well be a denial of justice and a restriction of freedom?
On this first day of extended sittings we are endeavouring to remove some of the legislative logjam along the road to June 30 so that we can celebrate our national birthday on July 1. It is paradoxical to move into this very sensitive area, which is also an area of personal conflict. We move into this area to try to help individuals. Mr. Speaker, I support this amendment without reservation or qualification. I am disappointed and surprised at what I perceive to be the minister's reaction to it.
I would like to deal with the subject matter under three or four different headings. As a lawyer I have practised before administrative tribunals on many occasions. As the minister will remember from his law school days, the nature of an administrative tribunal is somewhat of a jungle. Law students and law schools approach this subject with either trepidation on the one hand or fear and loathing on the other, because no one really knows how to deal with an administrative tribunal.
In law school we deal with remarkable things. We deal with extraordinary remedies, certiorari, mandamus, and that type of thing. There is no history, precedent or codification dealing with the operation of these tribunals. Some have operated effectively, and some have been disastrous. The point which I think is terribly important to make is that what is sometimes regarded as a cliche-justice must not only be done but must also appear to be done-is far more than a cliche. The perception of those who might find themselves in front of this tribunal is equally important as the substance of that tribunal's work. Let us remember that if those who might find themselves in the very extraordinary and emotional position of being before that tribunal are inhibited from doing so because of their perception of that tribunal, then this legislation is self-defeating.
I agree with the preamble of this bill. I do not think anyone in the House will challenge it, but if those who are potentially before the tribunal are deterred from availing themselves of its provisions, then this legislation is counter-productive. What would deter them from availing themselves of the protection of this tribunal? Well, certainly one thing would be if it is regarded as somewhat of a star chamber. There have been administrative tribunals of that nature, and I will name one, the CRTC.

May 31, 1977
Canadian Human Rights
The atmosphere before the CRTC prohibits the free expression of those who choose to challenge its rulings. We have CRTC hearings in Ottawa which decide the fate of people right across the country. Who is to come from my riding, from Calgary North, from the minister's riding, or from Annapolis Valley to appear before that tribunal in order to express freely their concerns about its deliberations?
Another one is the National Energy Board, which is charged with a terribly important function, but the atmosphere there is one in which no one but a lawyer would be comfortable. That is why I think we owe a great tribute to Mr. Justice Berger, who created a quasi-administrative tribunal and provided an atmosphere for people in all walks of life to be comfortable in while expressing their opinions about the future of their country and their communities.
With regard to appeals, it seems to me that the perception of an appeal to a group of confreres of the sole arbitrator has to be negative. As the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) pointed out, it is all in the club. At least that is the perception. 1 do not question the integrity of those people, but I can see what the perception would be. Why should the so-called appeal board overrule the decision of one of its fellows?

It is my view that a judicial appeal helps an administrative tribunal. An appeal to a court of appeal, for example, is almost like going to school for those who sat on the administrative tribunal in the original case because there are many cases where, without a lack of integrity or keen desire to be an effective tribunal, these people go astray. They get off on tangents. They do make mistakes, not just in law but also in their terms of reference. They make mistakes on the amount of evidence they allow in, and there are all kinds of things which lead an administrative tribunal astray. It has happened over and over again with innumerable tribunals. Therefore it appears to me that the right of appeal which is proposed in this amendment by the hon. member for Calgary North makes sense.
I think a good example of helping an administrative tribunal become more effective has been the system of possibly the best known administrative tribunal in Ontario. That is the Ontario Municipal Board, a very important administrative tribunal to the various communities of Ontario. Many of its decisions have been appealed successively, but I have never heard any of the board members say anything else but that those appeals were a great assistance to them in their future deliberations. Therefore, I earnestly solicit the minister's consideration of this amendment.
The minister must feel that there is some basis for an appeal, otherwise he would not have agreed in committee to an appeal to a board of three members. If he agrees in principle

I suggest that members of the House and the minister should acknowledge that there is a gap and a loophole in this proposed law which should be filled if human rights are to be protected. In all the provinces of Canada we have set up human rights commissions and passed human rights acts, and the idea has been to develop anti-discrimination programs within the jurisdiction of those provinces. Now, following the actions of human rights commissions and tribunals, we have established an administrative organization known as an administrative tribunal. This can come to the rescue and assistance of those in society against whom discrimination is practised. Mr. Speaker, we are embarked on a highly specialized area of endeavour.
What is the concept of this bill? It is the promotion and development of affirmative action programs, and the promotion and development of the concept of equal pay for work of equal value, both for men and women, without discrimination. It has been found from experience that this sort of thing is most effectively done through human rights commissions, tribunals or inquiries-whatever they may be called.
I quote the evidence given on May 19 before the committee by Professor Tarnopolsky, whom I have already mentioned. After the committee had wondered if human rights could better be advanced by the courts or by the sort of commission being proposed, he said, among other things:
The condition that had occurred right up through the enactment of human rights legislation in the provinces was that it was impossible to get redress in the courts
Canadian Human Rights
for acts of discrimination. The same thing was true as based upon the civil law of Quebec because it was based on the common law of the other provinces. It was specifically for this reason that the provincial legislatures all moved into the area of the administrative tribunals, as the minister mentioned .. .
The experience showed repeatedly in the province of Quebec where there are three cases, in Ontario there were two cases-and this was even after the enactment of the human rights legislation-and a certain number in Saskatchewan. But when the cases were taken to the courts, it was a totally new approach to comprehend the objects of human rights legislation. I would not want to say it was failure to comprehend because that would be unfair to the courts, but at least it was such a totally new approach that the provincial legislatures found it just unsatisfactory and moved to the field of the administrative agency.
The provinces of this country have had to legislate in this area. They have introduced anti-discrimination legislation and human rights legislation, and implemented this legislation through administrative tribunals, with limited rights of appeal. That has been found the only effective way to deal, in this specialized area, with the problems of those who suffer from discrimination. We are building on the experience of the ten provinces and that, exactly, is why we are proposing the provisions in Bill C-25. We are proposing the setting up of an administrative tribunal; the human rights commission and its tribunals. They will operate in a specialized area, with limited rights of review or appeal under the Federal Court Act, covering questions of natural justice, jurisdiction, errors of law and decisions based on erroneous findings of fact.
I suggest, in spite of the rhetoric from members opposite, that the approach embodied in Bill C-25 is based on the experience of ten provinces and ten jurisdictions in this country.
There has been some criticism within the committee and within this debate of the provisions of Section 28. I made it clear publicly and made it specifically clear in committee that the whole of the Federal Court Act is under review, including the jurisdiction of the court and the exercise of powers by the court in line with discussions and consultations I have had with provincial attorneys general.
If, as some members suggest, Section 28 is somehow deficient, which I do not concede for the purposes of this discussion, the time to amend it is when the Federal Court Act is before this parliament, which will be the next session.
The whole purpose of the Federal Court Act was to develop a federal court and a federal court of appeal that would provide a uniform judicial supervision over all of the federal administrative tribunals. I submit it would be unwise to go against that trend and go back to the old days where we had different rights of appeal.

Mr. Speaker, if we are going to accept this proposed legislation in a serious spirit-and I think all of us in this Chamber are committed to the spirit of the legislation-I think we should do our best to see that it is effective legislation. For this reason I must raise and support the argument of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) and reject the argument which has been advanced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford).
As I see his point, the Minister of Justice relies upon Section 28 of the Federal Court Act. That section has had difficulty
going in previous court cases, and apparently it is the subject of review as to whether it might be improved by amendment, although the minister has told us that he is not going to guarantee that any amendment will be proposed.
However, given the circumstances, if there is a question about legislation which may not achieve the purpose we want, or legislation which through an amendment, such as the one set out by the hon. member for Calgary North, would at least clearly spell out people's rights, I would say that it would be common sense to pass the amendment. If it adds surplusage to the legislation, at least its intention is in the right direction, and it does set forth something specific which is not otherwise clear at all in the law as it exists in Canada now. For that reason alone I must say that the hon. member for Calgary North has made his case, and the Minister of Justice has let the House down.
Second, I must support the argument of the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) that it would be helpful to have consistency within the legal operations of Canada.
